### Refreshed twenty-hypothesis tournament

These are qualitative priorities, not posterior probabilities, and several can coexist.

| # | Hypothesis | Evidence and next discriminator |
|---|---|---|
|1|Head4 routes input-token information differently across items|Leading testable account of concentrated residual; partition write contributions by input versus instruction tokens.|
|2|Head4's instruction-token routing changes with item identity|Also plausible; the same partition can distinguish it from input-token routing.|
|3|Query-dependent coefficients are the main source of variation|Test coefficient swaps with token values held fixed, using exact reconstruction.|
|4|Projected value content rather than routing explains residuals|Compare value and coefficient contributions at aligned input positions.|
|5|A shared instruction-conditioned mean plus small content-dependent correction suffices|Strong within-wording means for many tasks; fit a low-dimensional head4 residual only after identifying its source.|
|6|Wording transfer remains the main global limitation|H660 strongly supports five families; require new independent phrasings for generality.|
|7|Month succession fails because discovery coverage is narrow|H662 weakens coverage-only explanation but does not rule out larger representative data.|
|8|Head4 reflects calendar-item structure rather than succession computation|Possible despite low task competence; compare copying and other month operations on identical months.|
|9|Head4 serves broad factual/relational output processing|Capital and antonym patterns support exploring shared function; compare position-level writes across families.|
|10|Output formatting dominates head4 repairs|Open because exact task output is often incorrect; compare input-token and suffix-token contributions.|
|11|Head7 carries a distinct numerical component|Addition repair ranking motivates tests, not a label; compare arithmetic with number-copy controls.|
|12|Boundary and attention errors compensate|Supported by differing rankings and nonmonotonic repairs; retain both boundary controls.|
|13|A large geometric residual can be functionally inert|Prior geometry/KL differences support; assess projected writes against finite output effects.|
|14|A small residual aligned with sensitive directions causes most KL|Open; compare output-relevant directions with raw head residual norms.|
|15|Remaining error is distributed within a head rather than across heads|Head4 concentration permits testing low-rank residuals inside its128-dimensional output channel.|
|16|Several heads have redundant or opposing effects|Leave-one and single-head asymmetries suggest checking combinations before declaring minimality.|
|17|Exact attention transplants hide complex upstream computation|Certainly a limitation of these controls; predictors must avoid donor lookup and report full dependencies.|
|18|Mean output-write prediction is useful but not an intrinsic feature system|Consistent with wording/task conditioning; test independent datasets and transformations.|
|19|Output-KL equivalence differs materially from loss equivalence|H657–659 show concrete ranking reversals; retain distinct objectives.|
|20|A dataset-relative canonical description may require conditional units rather than fixed global vectors|Still plausible, not established; compare conditional head-write descriptions with fixed bases on prospective data.|

Next reconstruct head4 as a sum of token-position contributions, with explicit tokenizer alignment to the input, instruction and answer suffix. Verify that those contributions reproduce the native head write before patching them. Then repair role-specific residuals to distinguish content routing from instruction/format routing. Only after that should query/key versus value swaps be interpreted, because unequal prompt lengths make arbitrary positional swaps misleading. Retain all six families, task-competence caveats and independent fidelity/loss metrics.

No claim of successful task execution follows from repairing a natural task distribution. This remains a donor-informed audit of a conditional approximation; the original model and native receiver baseline are retained. The broad question of fundamental computational units remains open.

H658 established exact recovery when the incoming block9 state and all later attention writes are replaced by task-prompt values. H659 asks whether discovery data can predict those values without held-out donor access.

Run the full native/predicted/exact3×3 component factorial, plus an other-task control using pooled means from the other five families and the live-additive attention variant. It validates the intervention boundary and confirms that direct MLP replacement is redundant when its causal inputs are restored. The transplanted attention writes still carry substantial donor computation and are not compact or independent units.

Attention alone reduces mismatch in all families and outperforms MLP-context-only replacement in five of six (addition is the exception). All conditions remain at0% exact next-token accuracy on this held-out subset; natural task outputs are not necessarily correct.

The current result changes the approximation target. Rather than continuing to refine a separately transplanted MLP-context shift, test a data-based description of the block9 boundary change and later attention-output changes, letting MLP computation run naturally. Fit original-wording discovery means, evaluate second-wording held-out items, and cross predicted versus exact boundary/attention replacements to see which component limits transfer. Include other-task means and native baselines. Compare finite output KL, target CE and correctness independently. If simple predictions work, this gives a more causally coherent conditional surrogate; if they fail, exact recovery still supplies a useful upper reference without pretending the donor-informed states are an explanation.

This does not prove a global canonical form, smallest feature unit, semantic primitive, or end-to-end model compression. The exact information transplanted here is rich and input-specific; a useful representation must predict or compress it on independent data. The user’s broader objective remains open.

## H657 — Finite edits improve output fidelity partially; KL and task loss diverge

H656 predicted local derivative changes for copying→task instructions. H657 performs actual forward passes on the96 held-out copying prompts, editing only the final-position normalized inputs of MLP10–17. Frozen original-wording same-task means, second-wording discovery means, other-task means, norm-matched other-task means and constant-answer means are added to each evolving MLP input. Inputs are not renormalized after editing. The rest of the model runs normally, including downstream attention and normalization.

Two donor-informed controls distinguish adding a native context difference from replacing the evolving context. Exact-delta adds the natural task context minus the natural copying context. Exact-clamp interpolates the evolving input toward the natural task context; at amplitude1 it overwrites that input exactly. Neither replaces earlier computation or all attention. Both access held-out donor states and are controls, not deployable predictors.

All seven edit types use the fixed amplitude grid0.25,0.5,1. No amplitude is selected or tuned on held-out results. The same four held-out items per family and four forms are retained. Native copying and natural task outputs provide baselines.

**Output fidelity:** KL(task||edited) is the full-vocabulary KL divergence from the natural task-prompt distribution to the edited copying distribution, in nats. Smaller is closer; it does not mean more correct. The target task prompt can itself be wrong.

Full-amplitude same-task transfer beats pooled other tasks in five families, with antonyms again the exception. Controls and second-wording means have their own nonmonotonic responses. Exact-delta does not reliably solve the problem: successor full-amplitude KL0.550 is worse than native copying0.506. Exact-clamp does improve every family, but leaves nonzero divergence0.039–0.159. The exact context difference is therefore not a sufficient additive finite edit, and even exact later-MLP context replacement is insufficient to reproduce task-prompt outputs. Attention and earlier residual state remain plausible missing components.

**Task loss is a separate objective.** Target cross-entropy is minus log probability of the declared answer token, in nats. Lower can disagree with higher output fidelity.

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|

The clearest disagreement is antonyms: full same-task editing decreases target CE from5.387 to5.021 while increasing task-output KL from0.138 to0.157. The natural task distribution itself has worse target CE5.593 than native copying5.387. In plurals, the other-task edit achieves lower target CE5.409 than same-task5.758, while producing worse fidelity KL0.180 versus0.126. These are concrete examples of output-faithful and loss-oriented objectives ranking edits differently. No claim that either objective is universally preferable follows.

**Correctness:** every edited condition and both natural baselines have0% exact next-token correctness on this held-out subset. Candidate accuracy for native copy and natural task is addition0%, agreement50%, antonyms100%, capitals100%, plurals100%, successor0%. Most edits leave those rates unchanged; same-task amplitude1 changes agreement to56.25%. Candidate sets omit many incorrect outputs, so high candidate accuracy already present in copying does not demonstrate task execution. The broader panel's successor9.375% exact accuracy came from discovery items; it must not be transferred to this held-out subset.

These results move beyond derivative fidelity: some learned shifts produce useful finite changes in output distributions, but the evidence remains partial. The model retains its original weights, native earlier computation and full receiver context. This is neither a successful task transplant nor a canonical reduced model. It supports studying distribution-relative approximations with separate internal, output-KL, loss and correctness criteria, as proposed by the user.

Next localize the finite residual gap with an exact-factor intervention: donor final-position residual after block9, donor later attention outputs, and donor later MLP inputs, individually and jointly. A full combination provides a recovery check; individual comparisons reveal whether upstream state and attention are needed alongside MLP context. Use exact controls before fitting a more elaborate compact surrogate, and keep KL/CE/correctness separate. These are off-manifold intervention tests, not automatically causal shares of the natural task.

## Previous continuation: H656

## H656 — Copy-to-task local transformations transfer partially across wording

H655 tested how task-conditioned processing responds to verb/suffix changes. H656 instead changes the requested operation: copy the first input word/number → perform the task. Within each contrast, input, instruction verb and answer suffix stay fixed. Copy prompts are identical in the original and paraphrase panels. Target task prompts use the second wording. All six families, four forms and four held-out items remain, giving96 contrasts and288 probe evaluations.

Fit copy-to-task normalized MLP-context shift means on four original-wording discovery items. Evaluate these shifts on the second-wording held-out items. Compare: a mean fit on second-wording discovery items; original-wording copy-to-constant-yes means; original-wording copy-to-task means pooled over the other five families; and that pooled mean rescaled to the original same-task discovery mean norm. Norm matching uses no held-out target information. The norm-matched control tests whether advantages over pooled other tasks are simply differences in shift magnitude, though it does not control every family-specific nuisance.

For each contrast, retain the native copying receiver's attention, normalization derivatives and readout. Replace bilinear MLP operating contexts10–17 with native context plus the selected shift. Exact target task contexts provide the reference. Use the same seed654 three unit directions injected directly after block9. No output fitting or finite activation intervention occurs. This is a conditional change of local derivative operators, not a complete copying→task model replacement.

Relative effect error compares predicted versus exact context-replacement logit derivatives under receiver-probability-weighted centered logits, divided by the exact effect norm. No-change error1; lower is better.

| Family | New-wording mean | Original same-task mean | Constant control | Other-task mean | Norm-matched other |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|addition|0.210|0.455|0.965|0.703|0.739|
|agreement|0.273|0.649|1.036|0.856|1.037|
|antonym|0.369|0.818|1.042|0.846|0.869|

|plural|0.306|0.646|0.857|0.889|0.828|

The original same-task mean beats every control in all six family means: constant in284/288 individual cases, pooled other tasks in268/288, and norm-matched pooled other tasks in273/288. These repetitions share templates/items and are not independent trials. Antonym transfer is weak:0.818 versus other tasks0.846, with some individual errors above1 (maximum1.235). Thus average transfer does not imply uniform transfer.

New-wording means are better in all six families, with mean errors0.210–0.369. Cross-wording same-task errors0.455–0.818 show substantial residual wording dependence. Norm matching does not erase the same-task advantage. Exact context effects have magnitude0.186–0.569 times the native response, median0.290, so the relative-error pattern is not driven solely by near-zero effect denominators. These ratios are not causal shares.

This provides stronger evidence for task-conditioned transformations than the previous verb/suffix assays: a discovery-only copy-to-task shift retains useful directional information across a second wording and new items. However, other-task controls also differ in input/answer vocabulary, the paraphrases share words, and four families change token length. The transformation remains conditional on known family identity and native receiver states. It does not isolate a semantic primitive or establish a unique feature system.

Competence remains a separate limitation. Task top1 next-token accuracy is0% except successor9.375% in the second-wording panel; candidate accuracy ranges from12.5% to100%. Copying instructions are more reliably followed. Predicting the task prompt's local derivative does not imply executing that task or improving answers. H656 measures neither actual output distribution replacement nor finite intervention efficacy.

The next informative step is to test finite activation edits using these frozen mean shifts on copying prompts, allowing the rest of the network to run. Compare the resulting output distribution with the natural task-prompt distribution using output KL, while separately reporting target loss, candidate choice, and exact next-token accuracy. Include unchanged copying, exact target-context replacement, same-task means, and other-task controls across a fixed amplitude grid; do not choose amplitudes on held-out performance. Exact target-context replacement may itself fail to reproduce the task output because attention and earlier computation remain receiver-specific. That failure is informative about the limits of treating this MLP-context transformation as a computational unit. Finite effects must be measured rather than inferred from derivative fidelity.

## H654 — Task-conditioned context changes predict output effects beyond controls

H653 found held-out geometric regularity across six operation families with copy-first-token and constant-yes controls. H654 tests whether that task-conditioned advantage matters to outputs. It retains all six families: addition, agreement, antonyms, capital recall, plurals, and month succession. It uses four discovery items and four transfer items per family, and both Give→Provide and Answer:→Result: changes, each evaluated in two contexts of the other factor. This produces96 held-out contrasts.

Fit only the concatenated normalized MLP-context shift mean from the four discovery items, separately for family, control, axis, and setting. Compare own-task, same-input copying-control, same-input constant-control, and pooled other-task means. Exact context replacement and no replacement are reference conditions. The target context shift is added without renormalization across MLP10–17; receiver attention, MLP-normalization derivatives, and final readout remain fixed. No output fitting or parameter selection occurs.

Three seed654 orthonormal unit directions are injected directly into the final-position residual leaving block9. The same directions are used for every contrast and condition. This isolates the segment's operator differences; it differs from earlier block5 probes propagated to block9 and is not a replication of that exact probe distribution. The frozen mean/probe artifact and configuration are written before derivative evaluation. Native whole-block JVPs independently check the factorized native chain for every probe/contrast.

Error compares the predicted and exact context-replacement logit derivatives, divided by the magnitude of the exact context-replacement effect. The norm centers logits and weights by native receiver output probabilities. No-change error1; lower is better. This is local output sensitivity fidelity, not answer accuracy, finite-intervention KL, or a fraction of computation explained.

Own-task prediction beats every alternative in all12 family/axis means. It beats copy in286/288 individual contrast/probe cases, constant in284/288, and other-task means in286/288. Every own-task case has error below1; its median error is0.279, maximum0.722. Cases share prompts, templates and probes and are not independent statistical trials. No case is excluded.

The exact effect is not merely a vanishing denominator: its magnitude relative to the native response ranges from0.082 to0.793, median0.301. Context replacement is one conditional operator effect; this ratio is not a causal contribution to the full donor response or the task.

Copy and constant controls transfer better for suffix changes than verb changes in every family, replicating the geometric pattern functionally. Their average errors remain below1, consistent with a shared component, but the own-task means consistently predict better. This is evidence that instruction-conditioned differences matter to local output sensitivity, beyond the particular generic controls tested.

The results do not identify operation-semantic units. Task instructions have different words and lengths; the constant-answer instruction is not reliably obeyed; and exact task next-token accuracy was0% throughout H653 even when candidate selection was strong. Addition and successor candidate accuracy were12.5%, agreement50%, antonyms93.75%, capitals/plurals100%. Thus functionally relevant regularity exists even in poorly answered prompt families, but it could describe instruction processing rather than successful operation execution. That inference uses valid H653 declarations, not the withdrawn malformed H651 factual labels.

The strongest current account is a shared format-sensitive component plus an instruction-conditioned transformation. The next discriminating experiment should cross operation identity with alternative synonymous instruction phrasings and matched suffixes. Fit on one wording and discovery items, then predict a second wording and independent transfer items. Include copying and constant controls and account for token length. If same-operation transfer survives wording changes and exceeds other-operation controls, semantic-operation structure becomes more plausible. If it fails while within-wording transfer remains strong, lexical instruction structure is the better explanation. Measure native competence separately; do not select only easy tasks after observing results.

This remains a conditional data-based description, retaining the original model and native receiver states. It does not establish a unique canonical form, minimal computation unit, or end-to-end surrogate. Shared versus task-specific functional components should be tested before additional compression optimization.

## Previous continuation: H653

## H653 — Diverse operations separate shared formatting from task-conditioned geometry

H652 repaired the malformed factual labels and preserved frozen predictor transfer. It left only copying and capital recall as substantive task families. H653 broadens to pluralization, antonyms, capital recall, month succession, addition, and subject–verb agreement. Each has eight explicit item records, crossed with three instructions: perform the task, copy the first input word/number, or always answer yes. Each instruction is crossed with Give/Provide and Answer:/Result:, yielding576 prompts. The first four items per family are discovery, last four transfer. Declarations, prompts, targets, splits, runner hashes and configuration are saved before inference. Single-target-token eligibility and explicit item pairing are asserted. All prompts are retained regardless of competence.

This is an exploratory diagnostic panel with familiar/reused vocabulary, not a blind new lexical replication. Controls share the input and answer suffix but differ in instruction length and meaning; those differences are part of what must be disentangled. Agreement copying always targets The, so its candidate score is degenerate; constant-yes candidate scores are also trivial and are not reported as evidence of competence. Addition copying targets the first number.

**Native competence is uneven.** Candidate accuracy selects from the family's target tokens; top1 is full-vocabulary next-token accuracy, not full generated-response accuracy. All task cells have0% exact next-token accuracy in these instruction prompts, so candidate success must not be called successful free generation.

These results qualify this panel as an assay of instruction-conditioned processing, with task competence measured separately. Low scores could reflect prompt/task alignment, priors or actual inability; this experiment does not distinguish them. Constant-answer prompts often fail too, so they are instruction controls, not guaranteed no-computation states.

**Held-out geometry distinguishes the task-specific instruction from its controls.** Concatenate normalized MLP input contexts across layers10–17. Compute context shifts for Give→Provide separately at each suffix, and Answer:→Result: separately at each verb. Average shifts over four discovery items. Predict each of four held-out task shifts using its own task mean, the same-family copy-control mean, the same-family constant-control mean, or the pooled mean of the other five task families. No held-out fitting or rescaling occurs. Error is Euclidean shift reconstruction error divided by the true shift norm; zero-change error1. Values average eight item/context cases per cell.

Own-task means outperform all three alternative means in every family/axis cell. Control shifts nevertheless predict better than zero change in the displayed averages. Suffix changes are more transferable from copy/constant controls than verb changes in every family, suggesting a shared answer-format component alongside instruction-specific context. This is geometry, not a demonstrated output-relevant decomposition. The retained original model and supplied family identity remain essential. Task-specific instruction text and length could explain much of the separation without task execution.

### Refreshed hypothesis tournament: twenty competing explanations

Ranks are qualitative priorities, not posterior probabilities. Several can coexist.

| # | Hypothesis | Current evidence / distinguishing test |
|---|---|---|
|1|Shared formatting plus instruction-conditioned processing|Leading description: controls partially transfer, own-task shifts transfer better. Test composed output effects for both components.|
|2|Lexical instruction identity drives much of the separation|Plausible: task words and lengths differ. Compare multiple synonymous instructions within each operation.|
|3|Answer-introducing suffix has a broadly shared component|Supported geometrically. Transfer suffix shifts across tasks and measure output fidelity.|
|4|Stable mean change plus small item-dependent correction|Supported in prior copying/capital functional tests. Test discovery-only correction in these new operations.|
|5|Upstream state predicts the useful correction|Established within earlier two families. Freeze a predictor for new operation panels.|
|6|Internal regularity can persist without task success|Supported geometrically in low-scoring families. Measure functional effects and actual continuations before a behavioral claim.|
|7|Target vocabulary or answer distribution drives separation|Open. Use different operations with shared output tokens and balance answer frequencies.|
|8|Input lexical identity drives correction coefficients|Open. Cross identical inputs with competing valid operations and hold out lexical groups.|
|9|Instruction length or position drives separation|Open confound. Add length/position-matched wording controls.|
|10|Residual scale and normalization dominate differences|Earlier normalization-only tests weaker, not excluded here. Compare context versus normalization replacements.|
|11|Distributed context changes compose nonlinearly|Supported in prior broad wording shifts. Repeat finite-degree composition tests across new tasks.|
|12|Apparent higher-order structure mainly reflects shift magnitude|Prior scaling experiments partly support. Compare norm-matched shifts across task/control contrasts.|
|13|A few shared operator directions suffice across tasks|Unproven. Fit pooled discovery basis, evaluate held-out tasks and probes.|
|14|Each task needs a distinct operator subspace|Possible; geometric separation alone insufficient. Compare pooled versus per-task bases at equal dimension.|
|15|Small discovery sets hide transferable structure|Prior expansion improved rank3. Expand independent items before increasing rank.|
|16|Rare item-specific directions dominate remaining output error|Open. Compare average versus tail errors and stratify by item without dropping failures.|
|17|Downstream readout makes similar internal changes functionally different|Prior endpoint dependence supports. Compare internal fidelity, centered-logit error and KL separately.|
|18|Attention rather than MLP context carries task-specific differences|Not excluded; present assay records MLP contexts. Cross attention/context replacements.|
|19|Local derivative fidelity fails at finite intervention sizes|Open. Sweep intervention magnitude and compare derivative predictions to actual outputs.|
|20|No unique global feature system exists, but distribution-relative equivalence classes are useful|Consistent with task/context dependence, not established. Compare compression under internal, output-KL and task-loss objectives with independent evaluation.|

The next priority is hypothesis1 versus2/3/7/9: does task-specific geometry buy output fidelity beyond shared formatting, or mainly track wording? Use this frozen panel to compare exact task context shifts with own-task, same-input copy, constant, and other-task discovery means under identical receiver operators and probe directions. Report every family, with competence and output fidelity separate. This functional test can reject a geometrically attractive explanation before investing in more elaborate compression. Synonym and length controls are needed afterward to distinguish lexical wording from operation identity. No family should be removed merely for poor scores.

## Previous continuation: H652

## H652 — Correcting malformed factual pairs preserves frozen-predictor transfer

**Correction to H651:** inspecting per-item failures exposed a construction error. The runner split the string containing South Korea on whitespace. This produced separate South and Korea subjects, shifted subsequent country–capital labels, and omitted Pakistan because zip truncated to eight answers. The resulting37.5% factual candidate accuracy was invalid. The claim that the predictor transferred across failed factual recall is withdrawn. H651 raw artifacts remain unchanged for audit; its reports and accumulated research notes carry an erratum. Its operator results describe malformed prompts, not the intended panel. Copy results were unaffected.

H652 builds explicit country and capital lists and checks every factual subject–answer pair in every form against the H651 pre-inference specification. The intended pairs are Australia/Canberra, Chile/Santiago, Cuba/Havana, South Korea/Seoul, Iran/Tehran, Iraq/Baghdad, Indonesia/Jakarta, Pakistan/Islamabad. No predictor, basis, mean, probe, regularization, or item-selection rule changes. All64 intended prompts are rerun and retained. Most prompts had already been evaluated in H651, so this is a repair of the prospective design, not a second fully independent blind replication. The frozen predictors still have no fitting access to these items or their responses.

**Corrected competence:** candidate accuracy is100% for both families in all four forms. Exact next-token accuracy remains variable:

| Family | Form0 | Form1 | Form2 | Form3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|Copy|25%|0%|0%|87.5%|
|Fact|62.5%|0%|87.5%|37.5%|

Candidate accuracy is selection among eight target tokens; exact accuracy asks whether the target is highest over the full vocabulary. The latter is not complete-response correctness. ## H647 — A discovery-only residual span covers little of fresh context-shift variation

H646 was progress: a local functional eight-gain oracle improved fitted directions modestly but transferred poorly to a withheld direction. H647 tests additional directional structure rather than another scalar calibration.

For each of two task families and two template pairs, concatenate normalized MLP-context changes across layers10–17 into a9216-dimensional vector. Use only the four original H640 discovery items (indices0–3) and subtract the frozen H641 mean shift. Fit SVD directions to those four residual vectors. Because their mean is zero, their full span has rank at most three. Predeclare ranks1,2,3 and keep the same span for reverse template exchange. No output derivatives, probe directions, H640 items4–7 or H642 fresh items enter basis fitting.

For each H642 fresh receiver, compute its true donor-minus-receiver context-shift residual and project it onto the fitted span. Add that correction to the frozen mean shift and propagate the modified late operators. The coefficients are oracle geometric projections using held-out donor contexts, shared across layers and probes. They are not predictions and do not maximize output fidelity. Ranks are reported as a fixed sweep; no winning rank or subset is selected.

**The discovery basis fits its source data exactly but covers little fresh residual variation.** The rank3 span reconstructs discovery residuals within1.68e-15 relative error. On the fresh panel it leaves mean residual-relative norm errors0.951–0.962, capturing only about7–9% of residual energy:

These errors concern the residual after removing the already useful mean shift, not the full context change. Energy capture is averaged per example as1−error², rather than computed from the square of the mean error. Exact discovery reconstruction is expected with the complete three-dimensional source span; it is not evidence of generalization.

**Functional improvements are small even with donor-informed coefficients.** Error relative to the exact context-replacement effect is:

| Condition, donor input/readout | Frozen mean | Rank1 correction | Rank2 | Rank3 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|Copy matched|0.416|0.414|0.400|0.396|

Thus there is transferable structure in the small residual span, but its aggregate benefit is modest: donor-condition errors fall0.416→0.396 for matched copying,0.454→0.425 for broad copying,0.388→0.362 for matched facts and0.202→0.197 for broad facts. These improvements use true donor shifts and are not a new predictive result. Geometric projection can slightly worsen functional fidelity in individual cases or as rank rises, because the metrics differ.

**Interpretation must distinguish data coverage, rank and metric.** This test shows that the three directions available from four discovery items do not geometrically represent most fresh residual variation. It does not prove high intrinsic dimension, failure of all low-rank representations, or an information-theoretic limit. The discovery sample is tiny; concatenating all layers imposes coordinated coefficients; SVD optimizes Euclidean context variance rather than response fidelity. Functionally optimized coefficients within the same span could perform differently. Therefore this is a context-space representational test with functional evaluation, not a proven output-error lower bound.

The useful mean operator change survives this result. What remains unrepresented is much of the item-dependent correction around it. The evidence suggests separating a stable shared transformation from less well-covered residual structure, rather than declaring the entire operation arbitrary or claiming a single canonical feature has been isolated.

Next distinguish sample coverage from rank. Use the other four already available H640 items to expand discovery from four to eight while keeping the H642 fresh panel excluded from fitting. Compare the original rank3 span, a rank3 span learned from expanded discovery, and the full expanded residual span (up to rank7). Also compare the original mean with an eight-item mean so that mean estimation and residual coverage are not conflated. Treat this as a retrospective discovery-expansion diagnostic and retain oracle-versus-predictive distinctions. If expanded geometry remains inadequate, test a functionally weighted basis or more varied discovery contexts before training a coefficient predictor.

## Previous continuation: H646

## H646 — A functional gain oracle improves fitted directions but transfers poorly to a withheld direction

H645 was progress: geometric gain correction and one output-effect scalar left substantial residual prediction error. Those controls did not rule out a jointly output-optimized gain for each layer. H646 tests that larger family locally and verifies its actual composed effect.

At the frozen predictor's gain vector of all ones, the full response minus the response omitting layer l's shift is the exact partial derivative with respect to gain l. The fixed-state chain is affine in each individual gain even though it is not jointly affine in all gains. Use these eight functional directions from H643 to construct a local gain Jacobian.

For each of64 prompt contexts, fit an unconstrained eight-gain correction to the exact context-intervention target, pooling original/fresh0/fresh1 probes. Normalize each probe's squared-error contribution by its exact context-effect energy to avoid letting a larger response dominate. Keep fresh2 completely out of the gain fit. Fit receiver-input/readout and donor-input/readout conditions separately. Thus every gain vector uses target information for its own prompt and is an oracle, not a receiver-based predictive model.

Solve the weighted linearized least-squares problem with a fixed pseudoinverse tolerance1e-10. Then propagate both the full correction and a predeclared half correction through the actual composed chain. No clipping, line search or adaptive choice between full and half steps occurs. This is one local Gauss–Newton-style step, not global optimization of the nonlinear gain family.

**Fitted-direction improvement is modest; withheld-direction improvement is inconsistent.** Errors are relative to the exact context-replacement effect, with no context shift giving error1. Donor-input/readout results:

| Condition | Fitted probes: frozen mean | Fitted probes: actual full correction | Withheld fresh2: frozen mean | Withheld: linearized full correction | Withheld: actual full correction | Withheld: actual half correction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|Copy matched|0.434|0.359|0.361|0.346|0.345|0.334|
|Copy broad|0.437|0.414|0.505|0.499|0.498|0.496|
|Fact matched|0.374|0.345|0.429|0.441|0.441|0.429|
|Fact broad|0.210|0.165|0.179|0.188|0.188|0.176|

Receiver-input/readout results:

| Condition | Fitted probes: frozen mean | Fitted probes: actual full correction | Withheld fresh2: frozen mean | Withheld: linearized full correction | Withheld: actual full correction | Withheld: actual half correction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|Copy matched|0.428|0.356|0.348|0.329|0.328|0.320|
|Copy broad|0.420|0.384|0.433|0.435|0.436|0.428|
|Fact matched|0.387|0.361|0.413|0.425|0.425|0.413|
|Fact broad|0.205|0.177|0.228|0.243|0.243|0.231|

The actual full correction improves fresh2 in only28/64 donor-endpoint contexts and30/64 receiver-endpoint contexts. On average it slightly helps copying in some cells and worsens the two factual cells. The half step sometimes moderates the degradation, but was not selected as a preferred model. A single withheld direction is a limited generalization test; repeated contexts are not independent directional replications.

**The poor transfer is not mainly a failed linear approximation.** Fitted-probe cell means for linearized and actual full corrections agree closely; the largest individual difference in their error metrics is0.0149 for donor endpoints and0.0155 for receiver endpoints. Actual composed rollout therefore does not destroy a large linearized promise—the linearized held-out gain correction was already weak or harmful. This comparison concerns their error norms, not an assertion that the full response vectors are identical.

The numerical solve is also well behaved: maximum Gram-matrix condition number44.59, maximum relative normal-equation residual2.21e-15, and fitted gains range0.266–1.758. No extreme or negative gains are needed. Pooled fitted-probe linearized squared loss does not increase for any prompt/endpoint, as required by the least-squares solve. The optimization objective is pooled relative squared error, not the mean of relative error norms reported in the table, so individual probes need not improve.

The result weakens the hypothesis that the remaining context-shift error can be repaired by simple layerwise magnitude calibration shared across directions. It strengthens the priority of testing additional context-change directions. It does **not** prove that all gain-based explanations fail: more fit probes, repeated optimization, nonlinear constraints or a different gain parameterization might perform differently. Nor does it prove which directional representation is best. The tested local gain family simply offers limited benefit even with target access, and weak cross-direction transfer, so building a prospective gain predictor is not currently the most informative next step.

No predictive improvement is claimed. The frozen H641 model remains the validated predictor; these gains consume exact target responses for the same contexts. Fitting on three probes while withholding a fourth is a directional diagnostic, not a held-out-context evaluation. Existing task-competence, fixed-template and local-derivative limitations remain unchanged.

Next fit a small basis of **directional context-shift residuals** using only the original discovery items. Keep the frozen mean as a baseline, concatenate the eight layer residuals so coefficients describe a coordinated change across layers, and predeclare ranks1–3. On the fresh panel, use oracle coefficients only to test whether that discovery span can represent the missing shift and its functional effect across new probes. If even this representational ceiling fails, avoid training a predictor into an inadequate basis. If it succeeds, the next task is predicting its coefficients from receiver information without donor access. This separates basis capacity from coefficient prediction and retains strict discovery/evaluation provenance.

## Previous continuation: H645

## H645 — Geometric gain correction removes little of the residual context-shift error

H644 was progress: exact interaction-order expansion showed that small shifts admit accurate low-order approximations, while larger shifts require more orders. Once enough orders are retained, the dominant limitation is the frozen mean-shift prediction itself. H645 asks whether that residual error is mainly a magnitude mismatch.

Keep the H642 fresh panel, four probes and frozen H641 mean shifts. Use the true donor-minus-receiver normalized MLP-context change only for oracle diagnostics. For each receiver and layer, project that true change onto the frozen mean shift to obtain the Euclidean least-squares scalar gain. Also fit one shared scalar for the entire eight-layer stack. Both gains are shared across input probes; neither uses output responses. Compare their downstream effects with the unchanged predictive model and exact donor-context intervention.

Separately fit the optimal scalar rescaling of each full predicted output effect toward the exact effect, in the same receiver-probability-weighted centered-logit metric. This output scalar is target- and probe-specific and is strictly an oracle diagnostic. It is not a learned predictor and does not correspond generally to multiplying all context shifts by one scalar, because their composition is nonlinear in that scalar.

**Simple gain correction provides only modest functional improvement.** Errors below are relative to the exact context-replacement effect, so no context change has error1. Every oracle uses information unavailable to a prospective predictor.

| Condition, donor input/readout | Frozen mean | One geometric chain gain | Geometric gain per layer | Optimal output-effect scalar |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|Copy matched|0.416|0.368|0.364|0.357|
|Copy broad|0.454|0.440|0.440|0.431|
|Fact matched|0.388|0.389|0.387|0.373|
|Fact broad|0.202|0.203|0.202|0.190|

Matched copying benefits most: per-layer gains lower mean error0.416→0.364. Broad copying improves only0.454→0.440, and factual cells are effectively unchanged. A direct optimal output scalar still leaves0.357/0.431 copying errors and0.373/0.190 factual errors. That latter residual is the component of the target output effect not captured by the ray through the predicted effect; one output gain cannot remove it.

Receiver-only input/readout gives the same qualitative result:

| Condition, receiver input/readout | Frozen mean | One geometric chain gain | Geometric gain per layer | Optimal output-effect scalar |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|Copy matched|0.408|0.360|0.357|0.352|
|Copy broad|0.423|0.411|0.410|0.408|
|Fact matched|0.393|0.395|0.395|0.382|
|Fact broad|0.211|0.212|0.211|0.203|

**The context-space discrepancy itself is predominantly not a scalar mismatch in these cells.** Mean relative Euclidean context-shift errors before/after per-layer projection are0.388→0.357 for matched copying,0.436→0.427 for broad copying,0.402→0.399 for matched facts and0.267→0.266 for broad facts. Mean layer gains are0.885,0.920,0.962,0.988 respectively. Projection minimizes the context-space error along each frozen direction, but substantial orthogonal residual remains.

The gain that minimizes geometric error need not minimize output error. In factual cells it can slightly worsen functional prediction despite improving context-space reconstruction. This reinforces the need to judge any data-based representation by its chosen functional metric, rather than Euclidean alignment alone.

**What this does and does not establish.** The tested gains cannot explain away the current predictive residual, and a single output-effect scalar is insufficient. This supports looking for item-dependent directional corrections. However, it does not rule out a better eight-parameter functional gain model: jointly choosing eight layer gains to optimize final output error could exploit different directions and interactions than geometric projection. Neither the geometric-gain tests nor the one-output-scalar optimum is an upper bound on that larger family. No new predictive gain model has been fitted or validated here.

Refreshed20-hypothesis map:

1. Shared instruction-conditioned context shifts represent a transferable component of computation. Strong support from frozen prospective H642 results.
2. Item-dependent deviations in shift direction account for much of residual error. Supported geometrically and consistent functionally, but not uniquely established.
3. Incorrect overall shift magnitude explains most residual error. Weakened by the chain-gain and output-scalar controls.
4. Independent geometric gains per layer suffice. Weakened by their small improvements.
5. Joint output-optimized layer gains can substantially improve prediction. Open; requires a separate functional oracle test before learning gains.
6. Receiver features predict the remaining gains or directional corrections. Open; no such predictor has yet been validated.
7. Four discovery items give a noisy estimate of a truly fixed shift. Plausible contributor; more discovery items could improve mean estimates without eliminating item dependence.
8. Residual shift changes lie in a small reusable subspace. Open; fit only on discovery residuals and evaluate fresh items/directions.
9. A single direction per template pair is intrinsically sufficient. Weakened for high-fidelity prediction, though useful as an approximation.
10. A template-independent universal shift exists. Weakened by wrong-family norm-matched controls; broader sharing remains untested.
11. Input-direction-specific fitting explains success. Weakened: shifts were fitted without directional responses and transfer to new orthogonal probes.
12. A single layer is the computational unit. Weakened by H643 fixed ablations.
13. Independent layer contributions add into the transferable effect. Incomplete, especially for broad shifts; H644 identifies higher-order composition.
14. Broad formats require a categorically different kind of interaction. Weakened by norm-exchange diagnostics; amplitude explains a substantial part of the difference.
15. Final readout alone explains observed context dependence. Insufficient, though its effects depend strongly on the internal response.
16. Normalization is irrelevant to the mechanism. Too strong: earlier factorials show conditional contributions even though it is not the leading individual cross-wording factor.
17. Attention and MLP context play permanently separate semantic roles. Weakened by item-transfer coordination and format-dependent effects.
18. Candidate-set or competence failures explain all findings. Insufficient for validated response prediction, but still prevent claims about successful task algorithms.
19. Infinitesimal derivative fidelity guarantees finite behavior/loss fidelity. Unproven; local operator results do not establish a finite counterfactual model or accuracy improvements.
20. This representation is canonical across models or architectures. Unproven: the evidence concerns one model and fixed task/template contrasts, retaining native receiver context and full weights.

Next address hypothesis5 directly. The difference between the full predictor and each leave-one-layer-out predictor gives the exact local derivative with respect to that layer's gain at gain1, because the fixed-state chain is affine in each individual gain. Use those eight functional directions to form an oracle weighted least-squares correction, pooled across probes per context. First measure the linearized residual, then propagate the fitted gains through the actual composed chain to test whether the correction survives its interactions. Keep all target-informed gains labeled oracle. Only if this offers substantial improvement should a receiver-based gain predictor be pursued; otherwise prioritize directional residual models.

## Previous continuation: H644

## H644 — Low-order composition suffices for small shifts; broad-format higher orders are partly an amplitude effect

H643 was progress: the reusable context-shift effect was distributed across later layers and could not be reproduced closely by adding isolated layer effects. H644 resolves which interaction orders account for that difference.

At fixed native operating states, scaling each learned MLP-context shift by a shared scalar s makes each layer's tangent map affine: A_l+s K_l. A_l includes native residual scaling, attention and normalized MLP derivative; K_l is the learned bilinear-context change after the same native preceding operations. Multiplying eight such maps yields a polynomial of degree at most eight in s. This is an exact algebraic expansion of the local tangent model, not a Taylor expansion of finite activation changes or a fitted approximation.

Propagate coefficients recursively: at each layer the order-k coefficient receives A_l times its previous value plus K_l times the previous order-(k−1) coefficient. Final readout is fixed per chosen receiver/donor condition and linear in the tangent. Order1 sums all single-layer effects; order2 adds every ordered two-layer interaction; higher orders collect paths involving that many distinct shifted layers, with native operations between them. It does not identify an individual semantic circuit or selected pair.

The full coefficient sum recovers the eight-layer predictor; constant and first-order terms recover native and additive controls. Maximum relative residual discrepancy across these controls is4.59e-7. Direct computations at s=0.5 and s=−1 on the original receiver-input condition agree with polynomial evaluation within1.23e-7. These numerical checks support the algebraic interpretation.

**Pairwise terms approximate matched instruction changes well, but not broad format changes at their native shift amplitudes.** Errors below are measured relative to the full predicted shift effect, under donor incoming/readout conditions:

| Condition | Order1 | Through order2 | Through order3 | Through order4 | Through order5 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|Copy matched|0.2756|0.0479|0.0066|0.0008|0.0001|
|Copy broad|0.6457|0.3174|0.1154|0.0330|0.0069|
|Fact matched|0.3257|0.0740|0.0128|0.0016|0.0002|
|Fact broad|0.6257|0.2721|0.0869|0.0222|0.0039|

Matched pairwise errors average0.048/0.074, with individual maxima0.079/0.113 for copy/facts. Broad pairwise errors average0.317/0.272, with maxima0.467/0.588. Broad order3 still leaves means0.115/0.087; through order4 these fall to0.033/0.022, with maxima0.054/0.047. Higher orders are small but not literally absent. There was no predetermined acceptance threshold, so these values should not be converted into a categorical statement that order2 or4 is universally “sufficient.”

The pattern persists with receiver-only incoming/readout: matched pairwise errors0.048/0.076 and broad errors0.309/0.217. Broad order4 errors are0.033/0.025 in that setting. All template cells,64 prompts and four probes remain included; no order was selected for future prediction based on these observations.

**Approximating the predictor is distinct from improving its accuracy against exact donor-context replacement.** For matched copying/facts, pairwise truncation already gives exact-context effect errors0.417/0.393, close to the full predictor's0.416/0.388. The remaining error therefore mostly reflects the frozen mean-shift approximation, not omitted interaction orders. For broad copying/facts, pairwise errors against the exact intervention are0.534/0.328 versus full-predictor0.454/0.202; orders3–4 recover most of the lost fidelity. Occasional lower error than the full predictor is possible through cancellation of predictor errors and is not evidence of a more faithful context model.

**A post-result norm-matching diagnostic attributes much of the matched/broad difference to shift amplitude.** The eight-layer stacked shift Frobenius norms are21.07 matched versus47.50 broad for copying, and25.02 versus41.28 for facts. These norms depend only on frozen discovery-fitted vectors. Rescale each broad shift chain down to its family's matched norm, and each matched chain up to its broad norm, keeping its direction and per-layer relative sizes unchanged. Evaluate the already-computed full polynomial at that amplitude and compare truncations with that same scaled full effect.

| Rescaled intervention | Pairwise error at original amplitude | Pairwise error after norm exchange | Order3 error after norm exchange |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
|Copy matched, scaled up|0.0479|0.2231|0.0683|
|Copy broad, scaled down|0.3174|0.0632|0.0103|
|Fact matched, scaled up|0.0740|0.1964|0.0546|
|Fact broad, scaled down|0.2721|0.1152|0.0220|

Downscaling broad contrasts reduces pairwise error to0.063 for copying and0.115 for facts; upscaling matched contrasts raises it to0.223/0.196. Thus high-order remainder is not a categorical property of broad wording. Shift magnitude accounts for a substantial part of the regime difference, with remaining differences attributable to direction, distribution across layers, native operator geometry and endpoint conditioning. Equal Euclidean context norm is not equal functional operator norm, so this diagnostic does not isolate amplitude perfectly or assign an explained fraction.

The rescaled interventions are artificial counterfactuals, not observed alternative prompts. No new model parameters are fitted and no actual donor target exists for the scaled amplitude; their role is to test the mathematical mechanism behind interaction order. The original s=1 result remains the prospective predictor evaluated in H642.

The working explanation is a sequence of reusable context-conditioned operator changes whose products generate higher-order effects. Small changes admit useful low-order approximations; larger changes require more orders. This is consistent with ordinary composition of varying linear maps and does not require postulating an indivisible eight-layer semantic feature. Neither the polynomial nor its coefficients are a whole-model canonical form or a proof of computational minimality.

Next investigate the dominant remaining source of predictive error: whether held-out context changes differ from the learned mean mostly in magnitude or also in direction. Compare fixed mean shifts with oracle per-layer scalar gains along those same shifts, using held-out donor contexts only for this diagnostic. If gain correction removes most functional error, pursue a receiver-based gain predictor; if substantial error remains, identify item-dependent shift directions. Label oracle coefficients clearly and retain the already validated frozen predictor as the actual predictive baseline.

## Previous continuation: H643

## H643 — The transferable context-shift effect is distributed and composition-dependent

H642 was progress: frozen context shifts predicted component effects on fresh items and independently sampled directions without refitting. H643 tests whether that transferable effect belongs mostly to one later layer or to a distributed composition.

Keep the frozen H641 shifts, H64264-prompt panel and four probes. Evaluate eight fixed single-layer interventions and eight fixed leave-one-layer-out interventions across MLP10–17, with both receiver/donor incoming tangents and readouts. Retain the cached no-shift and full-shift controls and replay the full intervention independently on the original probe. No subset is selected, no parameters are fitted and no prompts are removed. This is descriptive localization on a now-observed test panel, not a new blind generalization test.

Primary ablation error is norm(ablated response − full predicted response) divided by norm(full predicted response − no-shift response), using receiver-probability-weighted centered logits. No shift has error1 and the full predictor error0. A separate metric measures error relative to the exact donor-context intervention, preserving the distinction between the predictor's effect and the true context-replacement effect.

**No single layer reproduces most of the full effect at high fidelity.** Under donor incoming/readout conditions, even the lowest mean single-layer error is0.825 for matched copying,0.885 for broad copying,0.889 for matched facts and0.910 for broad facts. These minima are descriptive across a fixed tested set, not selected models with validated future performance. The remaining single-layer errors are generally closer to1. A small local intervention can contribute to the complete effect without being sufficient in isolation.

**Every leave-one-layer-out condition changes the full predictor appreciably on average.** Mean omission errors range0.198–0.453 for matched copying,0.258–0.437 for broad copying,0.263–0.427 for matched facts and0.247–0.382 for broad facts. This supports distribution over several layers but does not prove eight layers are a minimal sufficient circuit: multiple omissions can interact or cancel, and a smaller jointly refitted representation was not tested.

| Omitted layer | Copy matched error | Copy broad error | Fact matched error | Fact broad error |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|10|0.453|0.437|0.427|0.310|
|11|0.404|0.382|0.367|0.301|
|12|0.328|0.341|0.311|0.282|
|13|0.280|0.297|0.265|0.247|
|14|0.246|0.258|0.279|0.249|
|15|0.221|0.262|0.263|0.280|
|16|0.198|0.260|0.264|0.373|
|17|0.213|0.337|0.299|0.382|

The relative influence varies by contrast: earlier layers10–11 are especially consequential for matched copying and facts, while layers16–17 are substantial for broad factual transfer. Endpoint choices also affect rankings. Receiver-only incoming/readout conditions yield the same broad conclusion: best single-layer mean errors remain0.825–0.889, and omission errors span roughly0.19–0.45 across cells. Thus distributedness is not solely an artifact of supplying donor endpoints.

**Adding independent single-layer effects does not reproduce their composition.** Construct the additive control as the native response plus the sum of eight single-layer response changes. The final readout is linear in the propagated tangent, so adding final tangents gives exactly that additive local-output control. Compare with the actual full chain:

| Condition, donor endpoints | Additive error versus full predicted effect | Additive error versus exact context effect | Full predictor error versus exact context effect |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
|Copy matched|0.276|0.495|0.416|
|Copy broad|0.646|0.763|0.454|
|Fact matched|0.326|0.486|0.388|
|Fact broad|0.626|0.634|0.202|

Matched instruction changes have a substantial but smaller nonadditive remainder (0.276/0.326) than broad format changes (0.646/0.626). The full composition predicts the exact intervention better than the additive approximation in all four averaged cells. Under receiver endpoints, additive-versus-full errors are0.278/0.619 for matched/broad copying and0.325/0.680 for matched/broad facts. This interaction is therefore present without donor input or readout.

The interaction arises within a local linear response calculation. Each layer's derivative changes linearly with its context shift, but multiplying shifted layer maps introduces products of shifts from different layers. It should not be described as finite-amplitude activation curvature or as an irreducible semantic synergy. Additive effects still carry useful information; they simply do not preserve the full predicted response closely enough in the broad-format contrasts.

The current result favors a reusable distributed transformation over a single localized “instruction neuron” or one independent layer contribution. Yet the eight vectors are a parameterization, not a demonstrated fundamental unit. The experiment says how this predictor composes, not which biological or semantic interpretation of those vectors is uniquely correct. All task-competence and component-versus-full-computation limitations from H642 remain in force.

Next test interaction order directly. Because each fixed-state MLP Jacobian is affine in a scalar multiplying its learned context shift, the eight-layer tangent chain is a polynomial of degree at most eight in that scalar. Propagate exact coefficients and compare first-, second- and third-order truncations against the full chain, with the full polynomial as a numerical recovery control and first order checked against this additive result. This can determine whether pairwise cross-layer composition captures the transferable effect or whether higher-order interactions remain necessary, without selecting a favorable subset on test results.

|---|---:|---:|
|copy / 0|62.5%|100.0%|

|copy / 2|0.0%|100.0%|
|copy / 3|87.5%|100.0%|

The research advance is a frozen, item-independent parameterization of a recurring operator change that predicts functional effects for new inputs and new perturbation directions. This is more than donor-operator lookup. It is still conditioned on the receiver's native context, uses the full original network, and only covers four known template-pair transformations across two families. It is not a unique canonical form or an identified indivisible semantic feature. The local derivative regime and retained endpoint conditioning remain material limits.

Next determine whether the transferable effect is concentrated in a few later layers or requires the distributed composition of eight shifts. Test fixed single-layer and leave-one-layer-out ablations of the frozen predictor, comparing each with the full predictor and exact context intervention. Use discovery items for any subset selection and reserve fresh evaluations for verification. This can establish whether a smaller reusable operator description preserves the demonstrated effect rather than treating eight layer-specific vectors as a unit by assumption.

## Previous continuation: H641

## H641 — A shared MLP-context shift predicts held-out operator effects

H640 was progress: the late-context/attention pattern replicated on new items and one-token, equal-length instruction contrasts. H641 replaces access to each exact donor MLP context with a simple fitted prediction.

For each family (copy/fact), template pair (matched/broad) and layer10–17, fit the mean change in normalized native MLP input over items0–3 only. Predict the donor operating context for any receiver as its own normalized context plus this mean shift. Reverse template exchange uses the exact negative shift. Items4–7 are excluded from fitting. This is32 discovery prompts and32 held-out prompts, because each item appears in four templates. The split and mean rule were fixed before this fit, but these items' H640 outputs had already been observed: this is retrospective item holdout, not a fresh blind replication.

The predictor does not fit output logits, response derivatives or any probe-specific parameter. It uses no held-out donor MLP context in its predicted path. The native receiver state, model weights, MLP normalization and attention are retained. Donor incoming tangents or readouts remain available in the explicitly donor-conditioned variants; receiver-conditioned variants use receiver components throughout except the predicted context shift. Test the same three probes as before. Exact donor-context replacement is the target intervention; no shift is the baseline. A control imports the mean shift from the other family at the same template index, rescaled to the fitted shift's norm.

The predicted normalized context is not renormalized: it is an additive approximation to a donor normalized vector. It need not lie exactly on the normalization sphere. This defines a local bilinear-operator approximation rather than a guaranteed naturally occurring model state.

**The mean shift predicts much of the held-out context-replacement effect.** The primary error is norm(predicted logit derivative − exact context-replacement derivative) divided by norm(exact context-replacement derivative − no-shift derivative), using receiver-probability-weighted centered logits. No shift therefore has error1. With donor incoming tangent/readout, prediction error is0.185–0.359 across the four cells, and all96 held-out prompt–probe cases improve over no shift. Receiver incoming/readout also improves in all96 cases, with mean errors0.186–0.395. These repeated observations are not independent trials.

| Held-out condition | Predicted effect error, donor input/readout | Other-family control error | Predicted effect error, receiver input/readout | Other-family control error |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|copy / matched|0.359|1.695|0.353|1.708|
|copy / broad|0.356|1.208|0.395|1.192|
|fact / matched|0.308|1.241|0.298|1.224|
|fact / broad|0.185|1.102|0.186|1.193|

The other-family shifts have the same norm but are worse than no shift on average in every cell and both endpoint conditions. This rules out shift magnitude alone as an explanation for the successful predictor. It does not establish semantic uniqueness: copying and factual prompts use different instruction words and formats, so the control changes several contextual attributes.

Results also hold across probe types. Mean held-out effect error under donor endpoints is0.315 for the historically selected original vector,0.285 for the learned-span probe and0.306 for the orthogonal probe. The mean model was fitted from native contexts without using any of these directional responses, although all three probe directions were previously studied. Generalization to new directions remains an explicit next check.

**Predicting the context effect is different from predicting the entire donor computation.** Under donor incoming tangent/readout, remaining full donor–receiver gaps are:

| Held-out condition | No context change | Exact context change | Predicted context change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
|copy / matched|0.616|0.342|0.415|
|copy / broad|0.690|0.336|0.416|
|fact / matched|0.749|0.342|0.436|
|fact / broad|0.635|0.204|0.228|

The predicted intervention generally preserves much of the exact intervention's benefit, but both leave other factors unmatched. With receiver incoming tangent/readout, predicted remaining gaps are0.774,0.965,0.827,0.853 for copy-matched, copy-broad, fact-matched, fact-broad respectively. Successful prediction of a component effect is therefore not successful end-to-end reconstruction of the donor response. In fact-matched receiver endpoints, the mean approximation is slightly closer to the full donor than the exact context intervention; this is not superior component fidelity, since unrelated residual errors can cancel.

The underlying context shifts themselves transfer approximately: held-out mean Euclidean shift errors are0.338/0.378 for matched/broad copying and0.358/0.238 for matched/broad facts, with mean cosine similarities0.946/0.927 and0.931/0.968. Functional validation is more informative than these geometric similarities alone, and is reported separately above.

What has been represented is a template-pair-dependent *change in a local operator*. For a bilinear MLP, changing context by mu changes its derivative by B(mu,DN_x q). Thus a shared context shift defines a reusable operator-change rule for different input directions, conditioned on receiver normalization. Across layers these local rules compose; the full output effect need not be additive in the layer shifts. The model stores one1152-vector per layer and family/template pair:32 independent vectors after accounting for reversal, while retaining the full original network. This is not whole-model compression, a unique canonical form, or proof of a fundamental semantic unit.

The evidence now favors a transferable component of context-conditioned computation over arbitrary item-by-item operator lookup. Its demonstrated scope is narrow: two task families, two fixed contrasts, four held-out items per family and three previously studied probes. Candidate-versus-exact-token competence limitations from H640 remain unchanged. No loss or accuracy improvement is claimed.

Next freeze these learned shifts and test a genuinely new item set and new independent input probes without refitting or choosing templates based on outputs. Include the no-shift and other-family controls, exact context replacement as evaluation target, and both receiver/donor endpoint conditions. This tests prospective prediction rather than another retrospective fit. If it transfers, then investigate how few context coordinates are needed and whether shifts can be predicted from instruction structure across unseen contrasts.

No new natural-text documents; FineWeb remains26,112. Broad goal active and incomplete.

## H640 — Prospective replication survives new items and one-token instruction changes

H639 was progress: later bilinear MLP context explained much of cross-wording transfer conditional on matched incoming response/readout, while item transfer often required attention and context together. H640 prospectively tests whether that pattern depends on the old items or broad formatting changes.

Freeze64 prompts before model inference: two families, eight new items each, four templates. Copy items are fish, horse, apple, chair, water, stone, flower, table. Fact subjects are Poland, Sweden, Greece, Turkey, Norway, Finland, Austria, Portugal; targets Warsaw, Stockholm, Athens, Ankara, Oslo, Helsinki, Vienna, Lisbon. Items and prompt strings are absent from the H633 task panel; some country names occurred in earlier language experiments. No claim of training-data novelty is made. All targets are single tokens with their declared leading space.

Matched copying templates are “Repeat this word: {}.\nAnswer:” and “Copy this word: {}.\nAnswer:”. Matched facts use “Name the capital of {}.\nAnswer:” versus “Give the capital of {}.\nAnswer:”. Each matched pair has identical token length, identical answer-introducing suffix, and exactly one differing token. This controls sequence length and answer position, though the changed instruction token remains a legitimate contextual difference.

Broad templates reproduce H633's contrasting formats on the new items: “Repeat the word: {}. The word is” versus “Copy exactly: {}\nCopy:”; “The capital of {} is” versus “What is the capital of {}?\nAnswer:”. Cross donors swap within each template pair at fixed item. Within donors shift item by four at fixed template. Use the frozen original/span2/orthogonal2 probes and the same full C/N/A factorial over blocks10–17, crossed with receiver/donor block9 incoming tangent and readout. All scripts and the prompt manifest were prepared before inference. No output-driven prompt revision or filtering occurred.

**The main conditional mechanism replicates, including for one-token changes.** With donor incoming tangent and donor final readout, exchanging bilinear MLP context C is more effective than normalization N or normalized attention A alone in every family/contrast cell. C lowers mean remaining-gap ratios from0.621–0.721 to0.205–0.336. Joint factors further reduce the gap, and the complete donor operator recovers the endpoint.

Values are means of per-example gap-norm ratios under receiver-native probabilities; they are not accuracy scores or causal shares. The primary table intentionally conditions on donor input/readout, matching H639. All other input/readout combinations are retained in the full result. This is not a claim that context replacement alone starting from receiver components reproduces the donor. The original, learned-span and orthogonal probes each have mean context-only cross-wording remaining ratios below1 in all four cells; the result is not solely driven by the historically selected vector.

**Attention–context coordination also replicates for item exchange, with an important conditional qualification.**

C+A produces large improvements for both families and both contrast sets. The earlier factual-item worsening from C alone replicates in broad formats (1.303→1.530), but not in matched-ending formats (0.883→0.727). Thus the claim that factual item transfer is always harmed by context-only exchange is false on this new panel. The more robust observation is that coordinated attention and MLP context outperform either alone for these item exchanges. This is still not a universal task/component division of labor.

**The matched contrast is smaller but well above the numerical recovery error.** Mean absolute weighted logit-derivative gaps for cross-template pairs are0.162 for matched copying versus0.339 broad, and0.252 for matched facts versus0.428 broad. Corresponding mean gap/native-response norm ratios are0.557/1.408 and0.714/1.262. Thus equal length and a shared ending reduce the contrast but do not eliminate it. The largest all-donor endpoint error relative to the gap is0.00132, ruling out tiny-denominator numerical noise as the explanation for the reported mean ratios.

**Candidate ranking must not be confused with immediate answer execution.** Every intended target wins among the declared eight candidates, but exact first-token accuracy varies:

| Family / template | Exact top1 | Candidate accuracy |
|---|---:|---:|
|copy / 0|25.0%|100.0%|
|copy / 1|25.0%|100.0%|
|copy / 2|0.0%|100.0%|
|copy / 3|100.0%|100.0%|

For matched copying, some top tokens capitalize the requested word or start “The”; the exact-copy labels deliberately preserve case. Matched fact prompts often start “The” or name another entity, and “Give…” has no correct immediate top1 targets. Broad explicit copying and declarative capital completion are each100% exact top1. First-token failure does not prove the full generated answer would be wrong, but candidate success does not prove it would be right. The operator result therefore concerns local response transfer across all these contexts; it is not a demonstration of universally successful semantic tasks.

The prospective result strengthens the hypothesis that bilinear operating-context changes capture a recurring component of wording-dependent late transformations. It weakens explanations based only on the old item set, changed sequence length or different answer-position suffixes. It does not rule out the lexical instruction token or continuation-format preference as the source of that context change. Attention–context coordination for item exchange also recurs, while the detailed effect of context alone depends on format.

Next move from native donor operators to prediction. On this frozen panel, fit an item-independent estimate of the normalized MLP-context change for each instruction/format pair using only the first four items. Predict donor contexts for the other four, then run the same downstream transformation without reading those held-out donor MLP contexts. Compare with exact donor-context transfer and no replacement, keeping input/readout conditioning explicit. If a shared context change transfers, that is a concrete step toward a reusable operator representation; if it fails, quantify identity-dependent residuals before increasing complexity. This is a new planned fit, not a result of H640.
