|middle/middle/middle|72.9%|+0.522|93.8%|+0.000|
|zero|97.9%|+1.227|100.0%|+0.696|

For the early recipient, position alone raises accuracy from 16/48 to 27/48 and the correct-answer margin by 0.402 nats. Key content alone changes the margin by −0.012, query content alone by +0.026, and both contents with early position by +0.004. All three changes give 35/48 and +0.522 nats; deleting the edge gives 47/48 and +1.227. There are content–position interactions: small content effects at the early position do not imply content is globally irrelevant.

The reverse positional substitution with middle query/key contents lowers middle-recipient candidate accuracy from 45/48 to 30/48 and margin by 0.520 nats. Replacing all three factors lowers accuracy to 32/48. These results support a position-sensitive harmful copying contribution in this head. They do not establish that rotary position explains the entire native first/middle performance gap: the recipients still differ through many other pathways, and even the full middle coefficient gives only 35/48 on the early prompts.

Candidate and full-vocabulary accuracy are separately retained in JSON. Middle native is 45/48 candidate versus 44/48 full-vocabulary correct; deletion is 48/48 versus 46/48. Early accuracies coincide for these interventions.

The current leading explanation is a reusable token-identity reader whose routing depends strongly on position, with contextual interactions and additional computation elsewhere. The simple cue-arrives-too-late account was weakened by H548. A full abstract recipient-selection mechanism remains unsupported; the model also fails arbitrary three-name mappings.

Next: freeze a prospective positional-response prediction and test several source–destination distances across competent binding and sequence-copy tasks, with agreement and sentiment as task-diverse controls. Separate virtual phase changes from physical padding/clause movement, report native competence and all failures, and test whether content explains prediction residuals. Avoid fitting a universal distance curve to this diagnostic panel and calling it generalization. Twenty-hypothesis tournament remains the broader research framework; this experiment only updates the position/content branch.

Audits: native coefficient replay max error 3.78e−7; identical source bus vectors across paired contexts; self margin error zero; finite results; unchanged source and cache hashes. Reused 96 prompts, no new corpus documents. H548–H549 together add 192 new prompts and 1,824 interventions. Tracked FineWeb total 26,112. Broad goal active and incomplete.

## Previous continuation: H548

## H548 — Earlier cue availability does not resolve harmful distractor copying

Test 192 new prompts: eight name triples, three role rotations, two givers, home/work absence cues, and cue-before versus cue-after the distractor name. The 96 pairs match the distractor token and position, total length, and final token and position. Wording and syntax differ, so this is not a pure semantic-feature manipulation. Head L14H4, distractor source role and five interventions were fixed before evaluation.

| Cue placement | Native accuracy | Distractor-edge deletion accuracy | Deletion margin gain |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
|home_before|31.2%|75.0%|+0.989|
|home_after|41.7%|85.4%|+0.917|
|work_before|20.8%|75.0%|+1.061|
|work_after|29.2%|81.2%|+1.037|

Candidate accuracy and full-vocabulary top-1 coincide in every condition above. Putting the cue before the name does not improve either cue family: home is 15/48 before versus 20/48 after, work 10/48 versus 14/48. Deletion transfers to the new prompts, reaching 36–41/48, but does not reproduce the earlier 47/48 rescue. This is evidence for a harmful contribution, not a universal repair.

Actual paired source-key, destination-query and joint swaps change mean correct-answer margins by less than 0.080 nats in absolute value; deletion changes them by 0.917–1.061 nats. These swaps affect other edges of the head too, whereas deletion alters only the distractor persistent-bus edge at the final destination. The simple hypothesis that the source key fails because the absence cue comes too late is weakened. The experiment does not prove the key lacks an absence representation, or identify the full routing algorithm.

Next H549 separates source-key content, destination-query content and assigned rotary key position in the earlier first/middle distractor pairs. All eight combinations will be tested as local bus-edge coefficient substitutions, with other edges and downstream computation live. This distinguishes candidate explanations of the selected pathway; it does not move physical tokens or establish a complete circuit.

Audits: 192 native prompts, 960 interventions; self margin error zero; all 96 matching assertions pass; finite results and unchanged source/manifest. No new FineWeb documents; tracked total remains 26,112. Broad goal active and incomplete.

## Previous continuation: H547

## H547 — Distractor-path deletion rescues the failure without adding answer names

Follow up H546's early-distractor failure on the same 144-prompt panel. The L14H4 distractor source was selected for this diagnostic after observing the candidate-mean rescue; this is not independent fresh confirmation. Freeze seven conditions before running them: self, candidate-name mean, unrelated-name mean, retaining 75%/50%/25% of the native contribution, and zero. Only the persistent-bus contribution from that source to L14H4's final destination is altered. Other paths, attention values and downstream computation remain active.

The unrelated mean uses eight specified names, all token-disjoint from the candidates in this panel. Deletion and attenuation inject no recipient-name representation. The head, source role and conditions are fixed; no per-example tuning is performed.

| Early-distractor intervention | Candidate accuracy | Full-vocabulary top-1 | Mean correct-answer margin change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
|self|33.3%|33.3%|+0.0000|
|candidate_mean|97.9%|97.9%|+1.2129|
|unrelated_mean|97.9%|97.9%|+1.2243|
|keep_75|52.1%|52.1%|+0.3093|
|keep_50|79.2%|79.2%|+0.6185|
|keep_25|89.6%|89.6%|+0.9253|
|zero|97.9%|97.9%|+1.2267|

Deletion reaches 47/48 correct, the same observed accuracy as candidate-name and unrelated-name means, versus 16/48 native. Accuracy improves progressively as the original contribution is attenuated: 25/48 at 75% retained, 38/48 at 50%, 43/48 at 25%, and 47/48 at zero. Correct-answer margins also improve monotonically in the aggregate. Thus candidate-answer injection is not necessary for this rescue. The deletion is local to one source/head bus edge, not an ablation of the entire head or distractor token.

The control conditions also improve candidate evidence when the distractor is later, but gains in candidate accuracy can differ from full-vocabulary top-1. With a middle distractor, deletion gives 48/48 candidate-correct and 46/48 full-vocabulary-correct, versus 45/48 and 44/48 natively. Parenthetical candidate accuracy remains 48/48, while full-vocabulary accuracy remains 43/48 under deletion. This distinction is retained rather than reporting only the easier candidate metric.

### Mechanistic implication and limits

On this panel, a value contribution from the irrelevant person's name through L14H4 causally favors an incorrect answer. Removing that contribution largely removes the early-distractor failure without supplying the correct name. This is a concrete, experimentally localized harmful computation. It does not prove a complete recipient-selection algorithm or that the same deletion improves general language modeling. The experiment uses the known distractor role to identify the source: it is not an automatic deployment-ready repair.

The conditional identity-reader account now explains both useful and harmful behavior: value copying can supply evidence for a recipient or a distractor depending on routing. The task label alone does not tell us whether that reader's contribution helps. Earlier successes with two names therefore should not be interpreted as proof of a general binding unit.

Leading alternatives for why the wrong source receives weight are: primacy or positional bias; insufficient context in the source key; an inadequate destination query; or narrative priors tied to clause order. A relevant architectural constraint is that the name's causal key cannot encode words that occur after it. In “C stayed home,” the disqualifying cue follows C, so any use of that later information must reach the reader through the query or another path. This constraint motivates a hypothesis, not a conclusion about the cause of the observed failure.

Next H548: move the irrelevance cue before versus after the distractor name while matching name and final positions, clause lengths and identity roles as closely as possible. Use fresh lexical combinations and keep L14H4/source interventions frozen. If earlier cue availability changes routing, cross source-key and destination-query states to locate the effect. Compare this with the primacy prediction; do not assume “irrelevance” has already been identified as a feature. Preserve fresh native accuracy and all counterexamples alongside deletion results.

Audits: 1,008 control interventions; self margins and candidate-mean replay agree within numerical error; unrelated donor tokens are disjoint from every candidate set; all outputs finite and source hash unchanged. The existing H546 panel is reused. No new prompts or FineWeb documents in this diagnostic. This goal turn added 576 new prompts across H545/H546 and completed 10,800 interventions across H545–H547. Tracked FineWeb total remains 26,112; broad goal active and incomplete.

## Previous continuation: H546

## H546 — An early irrelevant person exposes a localized harmful identity path

After H545's weak arbitrary-mapping competence, test natural three-person binding. Eight triples are rotated through active pair/distractor roles; either active person can be the giver. Only the active pair go to the market; the third person stays home. Place the distractor before the active-pair sentence, between that sentence and the giving clause, or inside a parenthetical after the repeated giver. There are 144 new prompts, with every name and giver role counterbalanced.

These are declared natural-language expectations, not a logical guarantee that an absent person could never receive a parcel. Score all three candidates, full-vocabulary top-1 and recipient-versus-distractor discrimination excluding the giver. Keep the four heads fixed and neutralize initial-giver, recipient, distractor and repeated-giver bus sources separately using the three-name mean. No successful subset is selected.

| Distractor placement | Three-way accuracy | Full-vocabulary top-1 | Recipient vs distractor | Both-giver blocks correct | Strong gate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
|distractor_first|33.3%|33.3%|33.3%|20.8%|fail|
|distractor_middle|93.8%|91.7%|93.8%|87.5%|pass|
|distractor_parenthetical|100.0%|89.6%|100.0%|100.0%|pass|

The later-distractor conditions pass competence, including the parenthetical case where the irrelevant name is more recent than the intended recipient. The early-distractor condition fails, with only 16/48 correct answers. A secondary earliest-mentioned-nongiver heuristic agrees with 32/48 early-distractor, 45/48 middle and 48/48 parenthetical model choices (125/144 overall). This post hoc observation motivates a primacy hypothesis but is not an independently confirmed algorithm.

### Causal localization

| Placement | L14H4 source neutralized | Correct candidate answers after intervention | Native correct answers |
|---|---|---:|---:|
|distractor_first|recipient|0/48|16/48|
|distractor_first|distractor|47/48|16/48|
|distractor_first|repeated_giver|16/48|16/48|
|distractor_middle|recipient|11/48|45/48|
|distractor_middle|distractor|48/48|45/48|
|distractor_middle|repeated_giver|44/48|45/48|
|distractor_parenthetical|recipient|38/48|48/48|
|distractor_parenthetical|distractor|48/48|48/48|
|distractor_parenthetical|repeated_giver|48/48|48/48|

In the failing early-distractor condition, neutralizing the distractor's value at L14H4 improves both candidate and full-vocabulary accuracy from 16/48 to 47/48. Neutralizing the recipient instead reduces both to 0/48. Neutralizing the repeated giver leaves candidate accuracy at 16/48 and barely changes recipient-versus-distractor evidence. L8H3 effects on that nongiver distinction are much smaller.

Thus the recipient and distractor value paths through L14H4 are behaviorally consequential, including a path favoring the wrong person. The result goes beyond an arbitrary fitted steering direction: it identifies a named source, a fixed head, a destination and a local value contribution affecting a specific failure. It still does not show that L14H4 alone performs association selection or that the whole model uses a single primacy rule.

The three-name-mean replacement is not pure deletion. It can introduce recipient-name evidence along with reducing distractor evidence. The source to alter is also identified from the experiment's declared distractor role, not by an automatic model repair system. Before claiming that removal of a misleading signal causes the rescue, test deletion, graded attenuation and replacement with a mean of unrelated names that excludes all candidates.

Audits: 144 native prompts, 2,304 geometry records and 2,448 interventions; source roles/token positions asserted, self margins reproduce exactly, all outputs finite, source/manifest hashes unchanged. Structured templates and role rotations are correlated; population-general performance is not established. No new FineWeb documents; tracked total 26,112.

## Previous continuation: H545

## H545 — Three-name mappings expose partial competence and weak association selection

The preceding goal turn made progress by rejecting a fixed query suppressor and finding little correct-value preference in two-name mappings. This experiment uses eight name triples, all six permutations, three cyclic demonstration orders and all three queries: 432 newly constructed prompts. Every key occupies each entry position across order rotations. Keep all four readers fixed and report every condition without filtering successful examples.

Score all three candidate names and the complete vocabulary. For nonfixed queries, also compare the correct target with the other nonquery candidate. Suppressing the query alone cannot distinguish those two. The strong competence gate requires >=75% of complete three-query blocks correct and >=50% intended full-vocabulary top-1 within a permutation kind.

| Permutation kind | Prompts | Three-way accuracy | Full-vocabulary top-1 | All-three-query block accuracy | Nonquery-rival accuracy | Strong gate |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
|identity|72|73.6%|73.6%|37.5%|—|fail|
|transposition|216|44.0%|44.0%|1.4%|63.9%|fail|
|cycle|144|61.8%|61.8%|6.2%|61.8%|fail|

No kind passes the strong gate. These results show partial ability, not total inability: cycle accuracy is 61.8%, above a fixed nonquery-choice baseline of 50% on this balanced design, but complete mapping execution is unreliable. The model never chooses the query itself on the 144 cycle prompts. Identity mappings produce 73.6% individually correct outputs but only 37.5% completely correct three-query blocks.

A useful failure occurs in transpositions, where two names swap and one is fixed. Accuracy is only 5.6% on the fixed-point queries, versus 63.2% on the nonfixed queries. This is consistent with a coarse nonidentity/query-suppression tendency rather than reliable query-specific association selection; it does not identify the full algorithm. A secondary most-recent-nonquery baseline has 50% cycle accuracy and matches only 36.8% of cycle model choices, so that single recency rule is not a sufficient account either.

### Causal source neutralizations

For each query and demonstrated value, replace one source-to-head persistent-bus contribution with the mean of the three name-value vectors. This removes some identity-specific evidence along that path while preserving shared name content, but also introduces equal candidate-name components. All other paths and downstream computation remain active. These are local sufficiency/neutralization probes, not whole-circuit necessity measurements.

On cycle prompts, neutralizing the repeated query changes the correct-versus-other-nonquery margin by only +0.0029 for L14H4 and +0.0045 for L8H3 on average. Neutralizing the correct value changes that margin by −0.7195 and −0.4782. Thus these value paths carry evidence that distinguishes candidate identities, while the query paths mostly act on the query identity itself. This does not show that the heads select which value is correct.

Indeed the correct value has the strongest identity-copying routing coefficient among the three values only 34.0% of cycle cases for L14H4 and 45.1% for L8H3. Uniform ranking would give one third; these are descriptive rates without population significance claims. The small L8H3 preference is not a complete lookup mechanism, and raw coefficient comparisons are only a proxy because token transformations differ across identities.

In transposition fixed-point cases, the query coefficient is suppressive in 100% of cases for L14H4 and 88.9% for L8H3. Neutralizing that path improves the correct-answer margin by +0.610 and +0.171, respectively. The same neutralization harms nonfixed cases on average (−0.151 and −0.038). This identifies a local contribution that can help easy cases while hurting fixed points. It does not establish that it accounts for the entire error.

### Direction update

The conditional identity-reader primitive remains useful, but strong claims about a general arbitrary-mapping algorithm are unsupported. Broad value copying plus context-dependent query correction remains plausible; selective association information may be elsewhere or insufficiently learned. Continuing to interpret poor arbitrary-task performance as successful binding would be misleading.

Next: test a more natural three-person narrative with an explicitly irrelevant person, while keeping three-candidate/full-vocabulary scoring and frozen readers. Vary distractor placement so a simple recent-name strategy can fail. Native competence and all failures must be reported, not used to silently choose a passing subset.

Audits: 432 native evaluations, 6,912 geometry records and 7,344 interventions, including self controls. Self correct/nonquery margins reproduce exactly; source token/position assertions pass; all outputs finite; manifest/source hashes unchanged. No new FineWeb documents; tracked total 26,112. Known names are recombined in new prompts, not claimed absent from model training. Broad goal remains active.

## Previous continuation: H544

## H544 — Mapping tests reject a fixed query suppressor and do not reveal a selective value reader

H543 strengthened the operation-linked interpretation of L8H3 across prose/list format, but two-name swap tasks can be solved partly by suppressing the query identity. This experiment compares identity mappings A→A/B→B with swaps A→B/B→A, in both demonstration orders. The local query syntax, names, name frequencies and positional layout are fixed across mapping type; only demonstrated target assignments change.

Keep all four readers fixed. For each prompt, intervene separately on the last query-name position, the value demonstrated for that query, and the other demonstrated value. Replace one source-to-head bus contribution at the final destination, allowing the rest of the model to respond. Two absent-token replacements measure relative copying/suppression; replacing the source value by the midpoint of A/B bus vectors neutralizes that source's A-versus-B identity distinction. The midpoint intervention is local and does not remove all information about the source from the model.

The run uses 32 prompt pairs (64 prompts). The 32 swap prompts repeat the two list conditions from H543; 32 identity-mapping prompts are newly composed. All examples and heads/sites are retained without selecting successful individual cases.

### Native competence is a material limitation

| Mapping | Demonstration order | Pairs with both intended contrasts correct | Full-vocabulary intended top-1 | Gate |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
|identity|ab|37.5%|68.8%|fail|
|identity|ba|0.0%|50.0%|fail|
|swap|ab|100.0%|100.0%|pass|
|swap|ba|100.0%|100.0%|pass|

Swap mappings remain fully competent. Identity mappings fail the operational gate in both orders, despite some correct individual outputs. Consequently these results cannot establish the mechanism of successful general identity-map lookup. They can still test what the selected readers do and how their local effects relate to correct-answer evidence on this explicitly specified task.

### Source-specific identity effects and neutralization

Positive third-token identity effects mean copying; negative effects mean suppression. Positive midpoint changes improve the correct-versus-other answer margin, while negative changes weaken it. Values average 32 prompt cases per mapping/site, including both demonstration orders and query names.

| Reader | Mapping | Source | Third-token identity effect | Midpoint change in correct-answer margin |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|
|L14H4|identity|query|-0.0984|0.0603|
|L14H4|identity|mapped_value|0.3610|-0.1719|
|L14H4|identity|other_value|0.3889|0.1845|
|L14H4|swap|query|-1.9098|-0.9422|
|L14H4|swap|mapped_value|1.8797|-0.9028|
|L14H4|swap|other_value|1.7934|0.8384|
|L8H3|identity|query|0.3669|-0.1773|
|L8H3|identity|mapped_value|0.6371|-0.3059|
|L8H3|identity|other_value|0.6068|0.2952|
|L8H3|swap|query|-0.7085|-0.3380|
|L8H3|swap|mapped_value|1.1773|-0.5487|
|L8H3|swap|other_value|1.1925|0.5283|

The fixed-query-suppressor hypothesis is not supported for L8H3. It suppresses the query in all 32 swap cases, but copies it in 25/32 identity cases. Neutralizing the query distinction therefore usually harms correct-answer evidence in both mapping types, contrary to the preregistered prediction that removing query suppression would help identity mappings. L14H4's identity-query effect is weak and mixed. This prevents attributing the model's identity-map failures simply to an unchanging query suppression rule.

Both readers copy demonstrated values, but they do not show a clear preference for the value belonging to the queried key. For L8H3, the mean correct-value minus other-value identity effect is +0.030 for identity mappings and −0.015 for swaps; the correct value wins only 17/32 and 16/32 paired comparisons. L14H4 differences are −0.028 and +0.086, with wins in 13/32 and 16/32. This does not support identifying either reader as a selective lookup mechanism on this panel.

The midpoint tests confirm the practical distinction: for L8H3, neutralizing correct-value evidence weakens the correct answer in all 32 cases per mapping type, while neutralizing competing-value evidence strengthens it in all 32. Both value paths carry behaviorally relevant identity information, including information favoring the wrong answer. Their coexistence is compatible with a pool of value evidence plus query-dependent correction, or with selection distributed elsewhere. It is not a complete explanation of natural task performance.

### Updated hypotheses and discriminating next step

The stable conditional identity transformation remains supported. Its task-level interpretation must narrow: it is neither a fixed query suppressor nor, from these measurements, a uniquely selective reader of the requested value. Local query syntax and name frequency do not determine its sign alone, since demonstrated mapping changes alter query behavior while those quantities stay fixed. Identity-map competence failure means the abstract “binding” interpretation is still unproved.

Leading alternatives now include: (1) multiple value identities are read broadly and query-dependent corrections disambiguate easy two-name cases; (2) true association selection occurs in other heads or upstream representations, with these readers supplying partial evidence; (3) template/recency effects rather than a general mapping algorithm explain some success; and (4) the tested mappings exceed the reliable capability of this model in certain formats. Keep all four live.

Next H545: introduce three-name permutations, including cycles and fixed points, in competent formats. With three candidates, suppressing the query no longer determines the answer. Freeze the current heads, score full-vocabulary correctness and all three candidate answers, and measure query, correct-value and competing-value paths separately. Compare selective association evidence with broad copying and signed query correction; report competence failures rather than selecting a passing subset. This is a stronger falsification test than another round of two-name sign confirmation.

### Verification and scope

768 geometry records, 2,368 interventions and 768 third-token contrasts. Source positions and token identities are asserted for each role; all values finite, self interventions produce exactly zero margin change, manifest/source hashes unchanged. These are correlated structured samples with hybrid local interventions, not population estimates or whole-circuit necessity tests. No new FineWeb documents; tracked total 26,112. The broad research goal remains active and incomplete.

The previous goal turn made progress by matching source/final tokens and positions and separating query/key contextual contributions. A prose/list heuristic remained plausible. He spoke to”; list binding uses “from A, to B; from B, to A; from G, to”. Tokenizer-selected “Note” padding matches source and final positions across operations within each primary format. New prompts reuse known names; this is format/operation transfer, not unseen model-training data.

| Operation / format | Reader | Positive routing coefficient | Mean causal third-token identity effect | Frozen sign predictions |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
|entity_binding/list|L14H4|16/16|-1.8720|16/16|

The locked coefficient-conditioned rule predicts all 192 leading-head third-token effects.

The evidence for L8H3 is stronger than a lexical/format correlation, but it does not establish an abstract binding variable. Local words around the source and query still differ. More importantly, with only two names, suppressing the query identity can favor the other answer without selecting an association. The new list task is mapping retrieval; it is not assumed identical to narrative entity binding at the algorithmic level.

Next: compare identity mappings A→A/B→B with swap mappings A→B/B→A under identical local query syntax and balanced name frequencies. ## Previous continuation: H542

## H542 — Context at both query and key selects the copying sign

Reuse H541's exactly matched standard-binding and position-matched-copying prompts: eight name pairs, two source identities per pair. Selected source and final tokens, their absolute positions, and the third-token alternatives match across contexts. Fix the same four heads and the H539 identity-map signs. No new heads or semantic directions are fitted.

Cross the origin of query representations (binding B or copying C) with the origin of key representations (B or C). Replace both actual query projections for the chosen head at the final position, and both actual key projections at the matched source position. Normalization and rotation then run natively. Other projections remain native and all downstream computation runs normally. These are actual Q/K swaps, not merely changes to an effective coefficient.

Query replacement can affect other source edges of that head; key replacement can affect other query destinations. The experiment therefore does not isolate one attention edge's total behavioral effect. To test the reader's conditional identity operation within each recombined state, additionally replace the designated edge's persistent-bus contribution with each third-token alternative, using the recombined coefficient. The difference between their output contrasts tests copying versus suppression with the altered attention state and all downstream response active.

### Context factorial

The table reports coefficients and effects for the two leading heads. Coefficient counts use the 16 matched name/direction cases; causal third-token results include both recipient contexts, giving 32 cases per row. Positive identity effects copy the injected identity; negative effects suppress it relatively.

| Reader | Query origin | Key origin | Mean coefficient | Positive coefficients | Mean third-token identity effect | Frozen sign prediction |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|L14H4|B|B|1.4791|16/16|-3.0179|32/32|
|L14H4|B|C|0.5754|16/16|-1.1764|32/32|
|L14H4|C|B|0.4014|16/16|-0.8144|32/32|
|L14H4|C|C|-0.0477|5/16|0.1008|32/32|
|L8H3|B|B|0.1405|16/16|-0.3005|32/32|
|L8H3|B|C|0.0322|16/16|-0.0690|32/32|
|L8H3|C|B|0.1084|16/16|-0.2339|32/32|
|L8H3|C|C|-0.1402|0/16|0.3008|32/32|

L8H3 switches to the copying sign only for C-query/C-key: all sixteen such coefficients are negative, while all three other combinations are positive. Transplanting either copying operand alone into the binding combination is insufficient to reverse the sign. The conditional identity operation follows the resulting sign in every tested recipient context. This locates relevant contextual distinctions on both sides of the edge, rather than solely in the query or solely in the key.

L14H4 likewise has positive coefficients in all mixed and B/B combinations, but C/C is weaker and mixed (eleven negative, five positive), consistent with H541. Do not generalize its role to unconditional copying. Both leading heads keep their second Q/K dot-product factor positive in every factorial case; the first factor supplies the sign changes.

The observed 2×2 sign table does not prove a discrete logical AND gate or that the bilinear cross term is uniquely necessary. Continuous changes in dot products, including additive changes crossing zero, can produce the same table. A secondary algebraic check illustrates the distinction: for L8H3, the first-factor additive extrapolation from B/B plus the two single-context changes is already negative in 14/16 cases, though the exact cross term makes it more negative on average. The valid primary claim is the actual counterfactual sign behavior of the four tested input combinations.

Across leading heads, the frozen identity rule predicts 256/256 third-token effects under actual Q/K recombination. L14H0 also predicts 128/128 with smaller effects, while L8H0 predicts 80/128 and remains weak/inconsistent. These repeated structured cases are not independent population samples. Correct signs do not imply exact prediction of effect magnitude or complete task accuracy.

### Research update

Together, H541/H542 rule out final-token identity and matched absolute positions as sufficient explanations for the leading L8H3 sign switch, and show that context-derived representations at both the query and key participate. They strengthen a conditional read–transform–write account: contextual query/key factors select a signed reader coefficient, and a relatively stable identity transformation determines what that reader does to token values.

They do not yet establish abstract “giver” or “recipient” features. Narrative versus list format, local surrounding words and contextual states still covary with the intended operation. Actual Q/K transplants are hybrid interventions, and upstream construction of those states remains unexplained. The broad objective is therefore incomplete.

Next H543: cross surface format and intended operation. Keep names and final “to” shared, add narrative copying (repeated sentences ending in “sent to A”), and list-form binding/retrieval (for example “from A to B; from B to A; from A to”). Retain narrative binding and list copying anchors. Freeze the heads and sign rule, screen native competence, and report all outcomes. This separates a role/operation-linked gate from a prose/list heuristic; local source cues and positional distances should be recorded and counterbalanced where feasible. Failed competence must not be treated as mechanistic failure. Only then consider transporting a learned contextual feature or pursuing source/key construction upstream.

The matching audit asserts equal source/final token IDs, source/final positions and third-token sets. Outputs finite and both source JSON and native-cache hashes unchanged. The previous goal turn made progress: H539/H540 supported conditional signed identity readers, while leaving a lexical-cue alternative. The last version is padded so its final token and nearest repeated-name position exactly match the binding final token and giver position. In this strongest condition, intervene only on that nearest repeated name; other copying conditions intervene on all changed value occurrences. All eight formats pass the competence gate. Every copying format has 100% both-endpoint contrast correctness and 100% full-vocabulary top-1. Binding anchors have 100% both-endpoint correctness and 87.5–100% full-vocabulary top-1. No pair is excluded. There are 80 new copying prompts and 48 repeated binding prompts, not 128 wholly fresh prompts.

Use the same name-valued third-token pairs across both tasks. ### Limits and next test

This rejects final-token identity and absolute position as complete explanations for L8H3 on the tested panel. It does not isolate an abstract relational variable: narrative versus repeated-list structure, surrounding words, padding, and earlier representations still differ. L14H4's exceptions further constrain a broad role interpretation. The result supports a context-derived gate, not a universal “giver” feature.

Next: use the saved native projections from the standard binding and position-matched copying contexts. Cross query origin (binding/copying) and key origin (binding/copying), replacing actual projections at the matched head/positions. Compare the two query/key factors and causal third-token effects. Keep both factor pairs and all heads frozen; do not fit a new semantic direction. This tests whether contextual information at the query, the source key, or their combination selects the sign.

## Previous continuation: H540

## H540 — A frozen signed-reader rule predicts new identity interventions and gate reversals

H539 found that the leading heads' identity maps were consistently negative, while routing sign determined copying versus suppression. Its secondary coefficient-conditioned rule is now tested prospectively. Keep the four heads and all identity-map signs from the original H539 discovery locked; do not refit on the new panel. The prediction is:

`sign(third-token contrast effect) = sign(locked identity-map sign * native routing coefficient * intervention gate)`.

The native coefficient is measured before intervention from that prompt's routing; it is an input to the explanation, not a learned prediction of how routes are constructed. This experiment therefore tests the reader's conditional operation, not a complete task algorithm.

### Design

Use another eight lexical pairs per task in three formats, giving 48 new pairs and 96 new prompts. Vary the third-token pair with the lexical item: eight name pairs for binding and eight non-name word pairs for copying. Some third-token words appeared in previous work in other roles; this is new prompt/role and combination testing, not a model-training holdout. All six native formats pass the competence gate. No prompt or pair is excluded.

For each head and prompt, replace its persistent-bus contribution from the designated source positions with a third token's value. Multiply that contribution by a gate of +1, −1 or 0. Only this source-to-head bus contribution changes, not the entire head's attention or query/key projections. Keep all downstream computation active. Compare the third0-minus-third1 output margin under third0 injection with that under third1 injection. A positive effect is relative identity copying and a negative effect is relative identity suppression. This does not assert that every individual token logit changes independently or that the full-vocabulary operator is exactly plus/minus identity.

Gate −1 tests reversal of the proposed operation. Gate 0 makes the two third-token interventions identical and provides an exact invariance control. Additional self interventions add zero attention change. The locked signs and complete manifest are saved before fresh geometry and causal evaluation.

### Prospective results

| Task | Reader | Gate +1 sign predictions | Gate −1 sign predictions | Mean absolute effect, +1 | Mean absolute effect, −1 |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|entity_binding|L14H4|48/48|48/48|3.1818|3.1351|
|entity_binding|L8H3|48/48|48/48|0.3007|0.3022|
|entity_binding|L14H0|48/48|48/48|0.1220|0.1218|
|entity_binding|L8H0|23/48|23/48|0.0006|0.0006|
|sequence_copy|L14H4|48/48|48/48|1.7414|1.7433|
|sequence_copy|L8H3|48/48|48/48|2.3228|2.2850|
|sequence_copy|L14H0|48/48|48/48|0.4394|0.4440|
|sequence_copy|L8H0|17/48|17/48|0.0035|0.0034|

The two leading heads predict all 384 nonzero-gate comparisons correctly across both tasks and both signs. The smallest leading-head effect is about 0.061 log-odds, well above observed self-control numerical error. Gate reversal reverses the identity effect as predicted despite downstream computation remaining active. All zero-gate comparisons agree within 3.6e-6.

The L14H0 control also follows its own locked signed-identity rule in 192/192 cases, with smaller mean effects. Its identity map is positive, unlike the two leaders, demonstrating that coherent identity readers are not unique to the selected heads. L8H0 predicts only 80/192 cases and has much smaller effects with unstable identity alignment. This control comparison supports an interpretable family of identity transformations; it does not establish that the leading heads are uniquely meaningful.

The 384 successes are structured comparisons across 96 prompts, with correlated lexical pairs, formats, directions and gate settings. They are not 384 independent linguistic samples or a population-accuracy guarantee. The intervention's supplied coefficient is measured on each prompt, so the result does not show that a task label alone determines the effect. Indeed H539 already falsified that simpler interpretation for some copying contexts.

### What this adds to the research objective

We now have a concrete conditional operation with prospective causal predictions: an identity-aligned or identity-opposing token transformation, multiplied by a signed contextual reader coefficient. The same map can produce copying or suppression when the coefficient changes sign. This supports read–transform–write relations as useful candidate units here, more directly than a fitted direction that merely steers familiar answer words. It describes a composite input/output relation rather than assigning meaning to one arbitrary internal coordinate.

It remains a partial mechanism. We have not explained how the native query/key computation chooses that sign, established the pathway's necessity in natural execution, shown that all source roles use the same operation, or derived a canonical ontology for the full model. The unit is tested on specific token-identity contrasts and hybrid source/head interventions. Other routes and MLP computations remain important, particularly for copying.

Hypothesis priorities: the source/reader account and reusable conditional identity transformations are now strongest for these two tasks. The earlier late-MLP answer-word-bias explanation remains relevant to H535; these findings do not rehabilitate those steering vectors as general features. The next plausible confound is lexical rather than relational routing: binding ends with “to,” whereas copying ends with a key token. The reader sign could partly follow that cue instead of the source's role.

Next H541: cross binding and repeated-copy contexts using the same names and the same final token (for example the copying key “to”), retaining the fixed heads and sign rules. Check native competence first. Compare routing signs and interventions while counterbalancing source order and positions. If the role-dependent sign persists with matched lexical cues, inspect the two query/key factors separately to locate where context supplies it; if not, narrow the interpretation to a lexical/context cue rather than a general role operation. These tasks directly distinguish hypotheses and should precede further compression work.

## Previous continuation: H539

## H539 — Shared readers oppose identity, with routing sign selecting suppression or copying

The preceding goal turn made progress by establishing a fixed-reader account and discovery-selected readers that transferred across the original task panel. Here retain L14 head 4 and L8 head 3 as leading readers, with L14 head 0 and L8 head 0 as fixed same-layer controls. No head is selected on the new examples.

Use the original eight discovery pairs per task to fit majority signs for two quantities separately: the head's token-identity transformation and the native routing coefficient. Then evaluate eight new lexical pairs per task in three formats. Binding formats include standard wording, reversed introduction order, and a shifted scene/verb. Copying uses new non-color values, a prefix variation and three repetitions. There are 48 fresh pairs (96 prompts), plus 16 reused discovery pairs (32 prompts). All examples are retained; no tokenization exclusions occurred. Each format passes the native competence gate: >=75% of pairs choose both intended answers and >=50% of endpoints have an intended full-vocabulary top-1 token.

### What is separated

For a head, compute its output projection applied to the difference between two initial token-value vectors. Measure this map's alignment with the unembedding difference for the same two tokens. Negative alignment means the map opposes token identity in this specific contrast. Separately compute the sum of native attention coefficients at the changed source positions, including the learned bus mixing coefficient. Multiplying map and coefficient gives the direction of the head's direct identity contribution. No semantic labels are fitted to hidden axes.

For causal tests, replace only the persistent-bus contribution from the changed source positions to one head's final attention destination, leaving every other contribution native and allowing all later computation to respond. Also replace those source values with either of two third tokens that are not task answers: Kevin/Brian for binding, stone/glass for copying. Compare the third0-minus-third1 output margin under third0 injection versus third1 injection. Positive differences mean copying the injected identity; negative differences mean suppressing it. This distinguishes a general identity effect from merely favoring the original recipient or answer token. These third-token interventions deliberately create hybrid states and are not claims about natural task accuracy.

### Fresh results

|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|entity_binding|L14H4|48/48|48/48|2.8164|-3.0839|48/48|
|entity_binding|L8H3|48/48|48/48|0.3393|-0.2447|48/48|

|sequence_copy|L14H4|48/48|8/48|0.7355|0.8520|40/48|

Both leading heads oppose identity for all 48 fresh directions in each task. In binding, both use positive routing coefficients at the giver position, yielding identity suppression. L8H3 uses negative coefficients in all copying directions, reversing its identity-opposing map into copying. L14H4 does so in 40/48 copying directions; the other eight have the opposite routing sign and suppress instead. Thus “this head copies during copying tasks” is too coarse. The computation depends on the actual coefficient, not simply a task label.

The coarse discovery sign predicts the third-token effect in 184/192 leading-head comparisons. A secondary, parameter-free analysis using the discovery identity-map sign multiplied by each fresh native coefficient sign predicts 192/192. This finer rule is not treated as the original coarse preregistered test; the next experiment prospectively locks it and adds gate reversals and more third-token identities.

The L14H0 control also implements a coherent identity transformation but with positive identity-map alignment and smaller effects. Its presence argues for multiple identity-reading pathways, not uniqueness of the two leading heads. L8H0 has weak effects and unstable identity alignment; its coarse sign predictions fail frequently. The result supports a structured source/map/gate operation rather than arbitrary head directions, but does not establish a complete or unique circuit.

Directions within a lexical pair and its three formats are correlated. Counts such as 48/48 are observed test outcomes, not 48 independent lexical samples or population probabilities. The new lexical and position variants strengthen transfer evidence; broader tasks and model-training holdout claims are not established.

## Previous continuation: H538

## H538 — An explicit token-to-reader computation reproduces the frozen bus intervention

H537 showed that a large fraction of the donor-bus effect survives when downstream routing, contextual values and MLP outputs are fixed to their native recipient states. Here derive and execute that conditional computation. Keep the H536/H537 injection layers and the full H533 discovery/transfer panels unchanged.

For the final query position, each downstream attention layer/head reads a weighted sum of the changed initial value-bus vectors at source positions. Apply that head's output projection, its learned persistent-bus coefficient, and the product of all subsequent residual mixing coefficients. Sum across all downstream layers and heads, add to the native final residual state, then apply the native final normalization, unembedding and logit softcap. In symbols:

`delta_final = sum_l,h,s [residual_gain_after_l * bus_mix_l * native_pattern_l,h(final,s) * output_projection_l,h * delta_bus_s,h]`.

The pattern is the model's actual product of two normalized query/key score factors; it is not a softmax distribution and can be signed. Native fixed contextual values and MLP outputs cancel in the difference. No predicted semantic label is supplied to this formula. Its coefficients do come from the full recipient-native forward pass, so this is a conditional model of an intervention, not a standalone replacement for the native model or an explanation of how those coefficients were constructed.

### Replay and source localization

Across all 64 task directions, the formula's answer margins match actual fixed-QKV/MLP intervention margins within 3.9e-6. The maximum final-hidden error is 0.0129 in absolute units but only 2.9e-6 relative to the intervention's hidden-state change; accumulated activations have large scale. Actual intervention margins also replay H537 within 3.9e-6. These are float32 numerical differences with the same bfloat16-rounded weights.

Every binding pair changes exactly one token position: the repeated giver name. Every copying pair changes exactly two positions: the repeated value token. The persistent bus difference is exactly zero at all unchanged positions. Thus the response formula localizes the manipulated source information as well as its downstream readers. This is more specific than calling an output direction a “binding feature,” but it does not yet prove whether the readers suppress the giver, select a recipient, or implement another transformation.

Exact replay is expected once the model is frozen this way and validates the implementation; it is not itself evidence of a discovered natural mechanism. The informative link is H537's result that the frozen response retains about 93% of unrestricted binding bus effect and 67% of copying bus effect.

### Reader selection and transfer

Treat each layer/head pair as a reader, summing its contributions across source positions. Measure the finite answer-contrast effect of each reader alone. Rank readers by mean donor-directed effect on discovery examples, freeze the ranking, and evaluate summed top-1/3/5/10 reader contributions on every transfer pair. Compare with 32 seeded uniformly chosen reader sets at each size. These random controls match reader count, not weight magnitude, spatial distribution or training history; they measure concentration, not uniquely semantic specialization.

| Family | Selected readers | Transfer contrast change | Fraction of all fixed readers | Range of 32 random-set mean effects |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
|entity_binding|1|3.0264|43.2%|[-0.0900, 0.5714]|
|entity_binding|3|4.2182|60.2%|[-0.1292, 0.5708]|
|entity_binding|5|5.2325|74.7%|[-0.0996, 3.2099]|
|entity_binding|10|6.6292|94.7%|[-0.1039, 4.2179]|
|sequence_copy|1|1.4340|31.4%|[-0.0243, 0.4780]|
|sequence_copy|3|1.8917|41.5%|[-0.0897, 1.4258]|
|sequence_copy|5|2.7557|60.4%|[-0.1037, 1.4377]|
|sequence_copy|10|3.8085|83.5%|[-0.2270, 1.6806]|

Binding's top reader is L14 head 4; its next two are L13 heads 5 and 0. Copying's top reader is L8 head 3; its next two are L14 head 4 and L8 head 4. Thus the same head can contribute to multiple tasks: L14 head 4 is first for binding and second for copying, while L8 head 3 is first for copying and sixth for binding. Layer/head numbers are zero-based. This overlap is consistent with reusable token transformations whose contextual routing determines their task role; it is not proof of a single shared semantic operation.

The top ten readers carry 94.7% of the fixed-reader binding effect and 83.5% of the copying effect on transfer. The best reader alone carries 43.2% and 31.4%. Selected sets exceed all 32 random-set mean effects at each tested size. All task directions are positive except one direction for copying's top-three set. Finite readout effects do not add linearly: selected-reader effects are computed after summing their residual contributions and applying final normalization and softcap. Fractions are relative to the complete frozen-reader contrast, not native accuracy or exclusive circuit shares.

### Hypothesis update and next falsification

The most concrete current candidate unit is a relation between a token-value source, a context-dependent signed attention coefficient, and a head-specific output transformation. H535 showed why a late task-steering vector alone can be misleading. H537/H538 instead provide an executable, source-specific causal account for a restricted intervention, with transferable reader choices. We still have not explained the native creation of the routes, established necessity, or shown that these readers retain the same operation across broader tasks.

Next test: separate the sign of the native attention coefficient from the token-identity transformation in the leading shared heads. Determine whether L14 head 4 copies or suppresses the giver identity in binding, and how its operation changes when reading repeated values in copying. Make those predictions using discovery only, then test fresh names, values, and role/position changes. Include matched reader/location controls and counterfactuals that distinguish suppressing a mentioned entity from selecting the intended recipient. Do not promote “signed token transport” to a general ontology until those tests succeed.

Artifacts retain all 7,200 individual-reader measurements, 4,256 selected/random-set transfer evaluations, 64 actual intervention replays, source-position records and final-residual contribution vectors. Source and manifest hashes are unchanged, all values finite, and zero bus change at unchanged positions is verified. No new prompts or FineWeb documents; tracked total 26,112. The broad goal remains active and incomplete.

The previous turn made progress: H535 weakened the general-feature interpretation of selected late MLP writes, and H536 localized larger binding/copying effects to attention and the persistent token-value bus. For each donor-bus substitution, compare five conditions: unrestricted downstream computation; recipient-native Q/K projections fixed; recipient-native contextual V projections fixed; both Q/K and V fixed; and Q/K, V plus MLP outputs fixed. Contextual V is the local value projection; the injected persistent bus remains changed. Include task donors in both directions, base-to-nuisance donors, and self donors. Six nuisance pairs have unequal token lengths and are excluded from all five conditions; no task pair is excluded. The same recipient-native projections are saved in memory before intervention, and hook counts are asserted at runtime.

|---|---|---:|---:|---:|

All 16 transfer task directions remain positive in every condition. Fixing Q/K alone retains 97.6% of binding and 99.7% of copying's unrestricted bus effect. Fixing Q/K and contextual V together retains 96.5% and 92.4%. Fixing MLP outputs as well retains 93.3% and 67.0%. Thus a large direct route from changed token values through recipient-native readers to the answer is sufficient in these interventions. Copying has more additional effect from downstream MLP response than binding under this particular conditional comparison.

These percentages compare mean answer log-odds changes, not task accuracy or unique causal mediation fractions. They are conditional on donor-bus intervention and on original recipient routing; they do not establish that native Q/K computations are unnecessary. Those computations supply the readers being held fixed. Nor is the additional effect of unfreezing a component a unique additive share: interactions among routing, values and MLP responses remain possible. The large intervention changes a stream available to many downstream layers.

The key update to H533 alternatives is that *reading token values through existing context-dependent routes* is more directly supported than *needing to change those routes* for these paired perturbations. This favors an explanation in terms of a source, a reader and its output transformation. It is compatible with learned features elsewhere and does not imply a complete native algorithm has been identified.

## Previous continuation: H536

## H536 — Binding and copying effects travel strongly through attention and the persistent value stream

H533 found small single-MLP-write effects for entity binding and sequence copying. Reuse their 16 paired examples each (eight discovery, eight transfer), including nuisance and self donors. Independently scan all 18 layers for three interventions: replace the last-position attention output, replace the last-position post-block residual state, or replace the entire persistent value bus. Choose the maximum discovery mean donor-directed contrast per family/component, then freeze the layer and evaluate all transfer pairs. Exclude terminal residual L17 from selection because it trivially determines the readout, and exclude terminal bus L17 because it has no downstream consumers. Both remain diagnostic controls.

The persistent value bus is initialized in the first attention block as a linear projection of its normalized token input. This precedes contextual attention: the bus initially represents token identities, not a contextual semantic summary. Later attention mixes its own value projection with this persistent bus using learned layer-specific coefficients. Injecting a donor bus after layer L changes the values available to future attention layers but leaves the current attention output and all earlier computation native. Later routing and MLPs are recomputed and may themselves change. This experiment does not hold routes fixed.

Bus replacement is allowed only for equal token lengths and uses aligned positions; all exclusions are recorded. Component scopes differ: a single attention/MLP write touches one position at one layer, while replacing the bus can affect many positions across every later attention layer. Their effect sizes therefore cannot be interpreted as an equal-budget ranking of components or additive shares of computation.

| Family | Component | Selected layer | Transfer donor-directed log-odds change | Ratio to native endpoint contrast | Absolute nuisance change | Positive task directions |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|entity_binding|attention|14|5.0438|65.1%|0.0441 (n=8)|16/16|
|entity_binding|residual|16|7.6883|99.3%|0.1468 (n=8)|16/16|
|entity_binding|value_bus|6|7.5035|96.9%|0.0350 (n=8)|16/16|
|sequence_copy|attention|8|3.2349|39.9%|0.5109 (n=8)|16/16|
|sequence_copy|residual|16|7.9573|98.3%|1.6898 (n=8)|16/16|
|sequence_copy|value_bus|3|6.8117|84.1%|0.7683 (n=5)|16/16|

The selected attention write carries about 65% of the binding endpoint contrast and 40% of the copying contrast, compared with the earlier selected MLP-write ratios of about 2% and 4%. Attention's task effects exceed nuisance effects on this panel. A late residual replacement carries almost the complete contrast, as expected for an accumulated state near the readout; this by itself does not localize the generating computation.

Replacing the persistent bus after L6 for binding or L3 for copying carries about 97% and 84% of the native endpoint contrast. That is strong sufficiency evidence under these hybrid interventions for the influence of early token-value information through downstream readers. It is not evidence that these fractions of natural task computation exclusively use the bus, that one layer performs the whole task, or that changing the bus has a small intervention footprint. The ratios are answer log-odds changes, not accuracy, KL recovery, or additive mediation percentages.

Nuisance effects remain much smaller than task effects, particularly for binding, but nuisance changes are not matched in norm, edit count or semantic specificity. Copying changes multiple occurrences of the repeated value; bus injection changes those token values throughout future attention. The native recipient routes can then update. A source-token/reader mechanism is therefore a plausible explanation, while the relative roles of fixed routing, changed downstream routing, contextual values, and MLP processing remain unresolved.

This raises H533 hypotheses 3, 4 and 10 (routing, source/reader relations, persistent value bus). It complements H535's downgrade of a general-feature interpretation for selected late MLP writes. The evidence now favors studying how information is read and transformed over simply naming a portable late direction.

Next discriminating experiment: at the frozen bus-injection layers, retain native donor-bus substitution but freeze recipient attention Q/K projections in later layers. In a separate condition also freeze their contextual V projections. Compare those conditions with the unrestricted bus intervention, using recipient-native replay and self controls. If most effect survives fixed Q/K and contextual V, direct transport through fixed readers plus residual/MLP processing suffices. If it collapses, downstream rerouting or contextual-value feedback matters. Save all native projections before intervention and report both directions for every pair; do not select new layers. This is a diagnostic on the existing panel and will still require new task variations afterward.

Audits: 3,591 interventions executed and 57 skipped for unequal token lengths. All 16 task directions per family/component were retained at selected transfer layers. Self swaps reproduce margins within 8.6e-6. Terminal residual swaps reproduce donor margins within 4.8e-6; terminal bus swaps have no effect beyond 5.8e-6 numerical noise. All measurements finite and manifest unchanged. Native model attention code was inspected to verify bus initialization, reuse and intervention timing. No new FineWeb documents or synthetic prompts; the H533 panel is reused, with tracked FineWeb total 26,112. No complete mechanism or canonical feature ontology is claimed.

## H535 — Changing the readout weakens the general-feature interpretation

Freeze the H534 number and sentiment MLP-write changes. Test 104 newly constructed prompt pairs (208 prompts) across six agreement formats and seven sentiment formats. Items and wording cross output formats; this is not a random population sample or model-training holdout. The original eight answer-token sets remain unchanged for anchor formats. New formats include pronouns, reflexives, other verbs, ratings, and yes/no questions with reversed semantic mappings. The full manifest and controls are fixed before inference; every format is reported.

Compare shared changes with their reversed signs, same-norm nuisance changes, four pre-existing random vectors, and a same-norm output-bias control built directly from the difference of original answer-class mean unembedding rows. Also project the shared change off the span of all original answer-token rows and rescale to its original norm. Test all ten modes at MLP12; test shared and output-bias modes at the final residual stream as well. The unembedding is the model's linear map from final hidden state to token scores. These controls match norm, not covariance or task performance, and are not optimized on these examples.

Each task format passes only if at least 75% of its pairs prefer both intended answers and at least 50% of endpoints produce an intended full-vocabulary top-1 token. Candidate-only success is distinct from operational competence. The modal invariance format requires the same verb form after “can” for both subject numbers and is reported separately.

Effects are signed changes in the two-answer log-odds toward the counterfactual answer, not accuracy changes. Values on failed formats measure contrasts only and cannot establish successful semantic transfer or its absence.

The original agreement format retains a strong shared-vector effect (1.424), but the competent pronoun format has essentially zero effect (−0.017); the competent reflexive format has a smaller effect (0.239). The simple output-bias control has larger effects on all three (2.148, 0.223, 0.706). Positive transfer to new verb forms is candidate-only evidence: both verb formats have zero literal full-vocabulary top-1 under the narrow declared output sets. This does not mean the model cannot perform grammatical agreement; other valid verbs may be its preferred completions.

Removing the original answer-row span leaves 79.2% of agreement vector norm before rescaling, but reduces the original-format effect from 1.424 to 0.135. Pronoun/reflexive effects become negative. For sentiment the retained norm is 93.1%, and the original-format effect falls from 1.067 to 0.386; the output-bias control produces 2.475. Direct final-residual insertion already moves the anchor contrasts by 0.776 for agreement and 0.417 for sentiment. Later model computation amplifies the effects of L12 insertion, but amplification is not proof of a semantic operation.

No alternative sentiment format passes both competence criteria. In particular, reversed yes/no and opposite-sentiment formats fail their native behavior tests, so they cannot adjudicate semantic reversal. Recommendation prompts sometimes emit an intended token but do not distinguish both polarities correctly. The original sentiment transport result survives, but its interpretation remains unresolved beyond an output-associated causal change.

The modal invariance control always prefers “work” over “works” natively, but neither is its top prediction. The shared vector still changes that contrast by mean absolute 0.672 (output-bias control 1.196), versus 0.074 after removing the original answer-row span. This is suggestive of grammatical-form bias insensitive to this construction, not a valid full-task failure claim.

Conclusion: downgrade the claim that these selected late writes are general number/polarity features. A write aligned with answer vocabulary, or an answer-amplifying operation, is a serious explanation; isotropic random controls were too weak to discriminate it. The evidence does not establish that all semantic information is absent, that output directions are the only explanation, or that earlier computation lacks reusable features. Strongly correlated grammatical readouts may share genuine number information, and the direct readout subspace is not a uniquely semantic/nonsemantic partition.

Hypothesis update: H533 alternatives 5 (answer amplification) and 12 (answer-token encoding) rise in priority for these late writes. Alternative 1 (reusable semantic features) requires a different location or stronger readout-general evidence. Alternative 2 (conditional operations) remains viable but needs a semantic prediction beyond operand algebra. Alternatives 3/4 (routing and source/reader relations) motivate the next binding/copying experiment.

Audits: 2,496 intervention records; no excluded prompts; all measurements finite; manifest and frozen source unchanged; self interventions reproduce margins within 8.6e-6 and KL within 3.4e-7. Negative KL at this numerical scale is floating-point noise, not a divergence claim. Shared vectors, output controls, complete-distribution KL/entropy changes and all per-prompt predictions are archived. Float32 computation uses bfloat16-rounded weights from the shared loader. No new FineWeb documents; tracked total 26,112.

## Previous continuation: H534

## H534 — Portable task writes coexist with different operand interactions

Following H533's eight-family screen, retain its five discovery-selected MLP layers: agreement L12, sentiment L12, capital recall L13, entity binding L10 and sequence copying L10 (zero-based). No layer is selected again. Reuse every eligible discovery/transfer pair. This is a mechanistic diagnostic on the H533 panel, not fresh confirmation on a new sample.

### What was tested

A bilinear MLP multiplies two learned projections of its normalized input, then maps their product back into the residual stream. Write these operands as L and R and the output map as D. Given a paired donor change (dL,dR), its exact output change decomposes as:

`D(dL * R) + D(L * dR) + D(dL * dR)`.

The first two terms change one operand at a time. The last is the finite cross term: information lost by adding the two separate effects. Evaluate each term, their sum without the cross term, and the complete donor write while holding the recipient's bypass and upstream computation native and recomputing downstream computation. These algebraic terms sum in MLP output space; their effects on answer probabilities need not add because downstream computation is nonlinear. A large cross-only effect is consequently not a unique fraction of the full effect.

For agreement and sentiment, separately average the discovery MLP-output changes from singular to plural or positive to negative. Freeze those two vectors. Add each to base transfer contexts and subtract it from counterfactual contexts. Compare against its reversed sign, a same-norm mean nuisance change, and 16 seeded isotropic Gaussian vectors of the same norm. No transfer example determines the vector. These controls match Euclidean norm, not residual covariance or answer-readout alignment.

### Results on transfer

Effects below are donor-directed changes in answer log-odds: how strongly the model favors the donor's answer relative to the recipient's answer. They are not changes in task accuracy.

| Task | Complete donor write | Without finite cross term | Increment from including cross term | Descriptive 95% pair-bootstrap interval for increment |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
|agreement|1.8437|1.5014|0.3423|[0.2616, 0.4249]|
|capital_recall|0.8757|0.6690|0.2067|[0.1510, 0.2613]|
|entity_binding|0.1454|0.0994|0.0460|[0.0374, 0.0522]|
|sentiment|0.8239|0.8249|-0.0010|[-0.0043, 0.0020]|
|sequence_copy|0.2886|0.2751|0.0135|[-0.0193, 0.0458]|

Agreement loses about 19% of this selected-layer donor effect when the cross term is omitted. Sentiment's effect is essentially unchanged. Capital recall and binding also have positive cross-term increments, though binding's total local MLP effect is small. Copying remains inconclusive. This distinguishes the selected local operations; it does not show that agreement is globally nonlinear while sentiment is globally linear. The normalized operands already include upstream processing, and downstream context determines how a write is used.

| Task | Shared discovery-mean change | Reversed shared change | Same-norm nuisance | Range of 16 random-direction means | Positive shared directions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|agreement|1.6320|-1.4891|0.0822|[-0.1767, 0.1260]|16/16|
|sentiment|0.9454|-0.9211|0.0855|[-0.1948, 0.2233]|16/16|

Both shared writes transport in the predicted direction across all eight transfer pairs, in both directions. Reversing the vector reverses the effect on every tested direction. Shared-minus-nuisance effects have descriptive pair-bootstrap intervals of [1.264, 1.868] for agreement and [0.833, 0.889] for sentiment. These intervals resample only eight deliberately constructed pairs, keeping the two directions together; they omit uncertainty from discovery, templates and model selection. They are not population confidence claims. Some random directions also move all answers consistently, which is why effect magnitude and control comparisons matter more than sign counts alone.

### Interpretation and remaining alternatives

The strongest supported statement is that a reusable *causal output change* exists within each of these two tested tasks. This is stronger evidence than low-rank reconstruction alone: the direction learned from one set of contexts changes behavior in other contexts, and its sign predicts the effect. It is not yet an identified semantic feature or a complete causal algorithm. A generic bias toward the declared output-token classes could explain this transport. New tests must vary the readout/output vocabulary while preserving the underlying number or polarity distinction, and compare against output-aligned control directions.

Reusable writes and conditional operations are compatible: a context-sensitive operation may produce a portable output. Here agreement's selected MLP operation uses a meaningful finite cross term, while sentiment's selected effect is approximately additive for these paired changes. The checkpoint's Left and Right coordinates are not claimed to be canonical semantic axes.

The next high-information tests are (1) task/readout-crossed transfer to distinguish a semantic feature from an answer-word bias, and (2) attention/residual/value-bus localization for binding and copying, whose single-MLP effects were small. Broader multi-layer hypotheses remain open. H533's twenty-hypothesis list remains the working alternatives; prioritize reusable features, conditional operations, routing, and source/reader dependence rather than another compression sweep.

### Verification and scope

The 960 operand interventions and 608 transport interventions are finite; complete-donor replay agrees with H533 to within 6.7e-6 in margin, and self swaps agree within 6.2e-6. The algebra was independently checked in float64 using the same rounded weights as inference: maximum algebra error 5.7e-14, maximum relative L2 discrepancy from the actual float32 donor-write difference 1.5e-6. Initial comparison against unrounded checkpoint weights was corrected to match the inference loader. Inference uses float32 computation after the shared loader converts checkpoint weights to bfloat16; it is not unrounded float32 checkpoint inference.

Both runs use a small synthetic prompt suite. Discovery and transfer vary templates and items together, and some vocabulary overlaps; a crossed design is still needed. The exploratory negation examples also have pragmatic ambiguity (for example, “not wonderful” need not mean wholly negative), and ambiguous-word probes do not specify uniquely required completions. Their gate failures are format-specific observations. No new FineWeb documents were consumed; tracked total remains 26,112. Source and manifest hashes, per-intervention results, operands, frozen transport vectors and the numerical audit are archived. The broad research goal remains active.

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|

Single selected MLP writes move about 22% of the native agreement contrast and 32% of sentiment contrast on transfer; capital recall is about 9%. Binding and copying are only about 2% and 4%. These are ratios of aggregate contrast changes, not fractions of task accuracy, necessary computation or uniquely mediated information. Whole-output swaps are sufficiency probes under hybrid states, not necessity tests. Copying's nuisance effect is comparable to its task effect, so this localization is not selective evidence for a copying operation. Nuisance edits are not matched in edit count or activation norm, and only base-to-nuisance is tested; comparisons are descriptive.

This prioritizes reusable feature changes versus conditional operations for agreement/sentiment. It prioritizes attention, residual and value-bus paths for binding/copying. It does not establish that those paths are responsible: they have not been tested in this run. The source of a whole MLP output's information remains unidentified.

Audits: native custom forward matches the existing native forward exactly; self swaps change margins by at most 6.68e-06; all causal margins finite; manifest unchanged; 0 excluded pairs. The 3,040 intervention records include all discovery layers and frozen-layer transfer, nuisance and self controls. Full prompt manifest, per-prompt predictions and per-intervention margins are archived.

Next experiment: freeze the selected layers and dissect left/right bilinear operand swaps, including their exact cross term. Separately fit shared number/polarity write changes on discovery only and test transport to transfer contexts against nuisance and random controls. Neither experiment presumes that checkpoint operand coordinates are unique semantic features.

### Twenty competing explanations and discriminating tests

1. Reusable semantic changes are mixed across neuron coordinates. Test whether a discovery-mean number/polarity write transfers to unseen items, against matched nuisance and random directions.
2. A context-dependent bilinear operation is the useful unit. Swap left and right operands separately; test the finite cross term and transport across receivers.
3. Information routing dominates binding and copying. Compare attention-write swaps with MLP-write swaps at every layer on discovery and frozen selected layers on transfer.
4. Features become usable only at a downstream reader. Preserve a source change while replacing or varying the receiving state; test output predictions beyond reconstruction.
5. MLPs mostly amplify already-selected answers. Compare task contrast before/after each MLP and predict effects from native answer alignment; agreement with this alone is not semantic identification.
6. Whole-write effects come from generic confidence changes. Measure complete distribution KL, entropy, and effects on unrelated tokens, alongside answer contrasts.
7. Several layers implement redundant versions of the same operation. Compare isolated and jointly patched layers; look for subadditive effects.
8. Several layers implement a sequence of necessary operations. Compare combinations and path-specific interventions; look for order-dependent interactions.
9. The residual bypass carries most binding information. Compare residual-stream swaps, attention writes and MLP writes without conflating their differing scopes.
10. The persistent attention value bus carries important information missed by residual-only swaps. Intervene on it separately with native replay controls.
11. Within-task features transfer but cross-task universality is limited. Freeze task-specific transformations and evaluate semantically aligned cross-task conditions.
12. Apparent feature directions encode answer tokens. Hold the relation fixed while changing output vocabulary; test counterbalanced mappings.
13. Apparent relations encode particular prompt templates. Hold lexicon fixed across templates and template fixed across lexicons in a crossed design.
14. The competence gate hides brittle cases. Report every declared prompt and evaluate failure cases separately without using them to select mechanisms.
15. A low-dimensional feature is represented nonlinearly. Compare fixed vector transport with receiver-conditioned transformations on strictly separate fit and evaluation sets.
16. A useful unit is a distributed subspace rather than a neuron. Compare causal subspace interventions with matched controls; do not infer semantics from rank alone.
17. Changes in normalization create apparent operand interactions. Separate pre-normalization effects from algebraic interactions in the already normalized bilinear operands.
18. Semantically equivalent coordinates are non-unique. Test whether different fitted coordinates predict the same held-out interventions; interpret the equivalence class rather than naming axes.
19. Off-distribution hybrids exaggerate causal effects. Compare native donor swaps with interpolation paths, endpoint controls and norm-matched nuisance swaps.
20. The chosen local units are genuinely insufficient. Escalate to multi-position, multi-layer source-to-reader paths only if simpler frozen explanations fail on new examples.

Priority: hypotheses 1–4 are the leading working explanations, with 5, 12, 13, 17 and 19 as immediate alternatives/controls. This ranking is qualitative; the present observations do not identify a winner.

## H531 — Context-dependent updates are harder to preserve than whole source writes

For each document and short history L=32/64/96, define delta=s_128−s_L using summed L17 attention writes. Hold the native128-token pre-MLP receiver fixed and substitute the source write s_L+A(delta). The resulting pre-MLP input is p_128−(delta−A(delta)), evaluated through the full residual bypass plus native MLP and readout. A is a frozen H522 PCA/Fisher map at rank36/144/576. The old reconstruction mean cancels and is not inserted.

Zero-map removal replaces the long-context source with the short-context source while keeping the long-context receiver's other components. Identity preserves the complete update and must reproduce native predictions. This is an artificial hybrid intervention on the final attention write, not the actual short-context model or total contribution of extra context. Earlier residual computation and receiver sensitivity remain long-context quantities.

| Short history | Zero-update KL | PCA36 recovery | Fisher36 recovery | PCA144 recovery | Fisher144 recovery | PCA576 recovery | Fisher576 recovery |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|32|0.00276475|57.23%|60.76%|82.25%|84.01%|97.65%|98.20%|

The raw geometry agrees with that limitation: Fisher36 retains about56.7–59.1% of delta energy, while PCA36 retains60.1–62.3%. Fisher nevertheless has better behavioral recovery for all tested ranks/gaps. Behavioral weighting helps, but does not make the contextual update a tiny-rank object in this fixed representation.

The zero-update KL shrinks from0.002765 for32→128 to0.001178 for64→128 and0.000419 for96→128.
