## H528 — Observed label-gradient variability has approximately the teacher-implied scale

On the2,048 H527 contexts, freeze both gain directions and the same rank36 compressed map. Let p be the original model's token distribution and J_y the derivative of the compressed model's soft-capped logit for token y along a gain direction. The observed-label contrast CE−KL is E_p[J]−J_y: normalization terms cancel. If y were drawn from p, its conditional mean would be zero and its conditional covariance would be Cov_p(J). Compute this covariance exactly by summing over the vocabulary, not sampling labels.

This is a model-implied reference, not the assumption that p is the true next-token distribution. Under independent teacher-label draws conditional on these contexts, the covariance of the average is sum_i Cov_i/n². Actual empirical across-document variability may also include context-dependent mean differences and distributional mismatch.

| Gain direction | Observed mean contrast | Teacher-implied mean SE | Empirical mean SE | Empirical / teacher variance | Mean / teacher SE |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|KL_direction|-0.00094460|0.00125643|0.00127646|1.032|-0.752|
|contrast_direction|+0.00098199|0.00086313|0.00092499|1.148|+1.138|

Observed contrast variance is about1.03 times the teacher reference along the KL direction and1.15 times along the contrast direction. The corresponding means are−0.75 and+1.14 reference standard errors from zero. Thus the observed failure to reproduce a CE-specific direction has roughly the noise scale expected from one observed token per context. This does not establish calibration, prove a zero task signal, or show that KL and CE share an optimum. The ratios have not been tested for equivalence; reference-SE standardized means are descriptive, not calibrated p-values.

The table concerns CE−KL along both directions. In particular, its negative mean along the KL direction does not contradict H527's positive KL-gradient projection; these are different gradients. CE gradients combine both terms.

Conditional variance is concentrated across contexts: the highest21 of2,048 contexts contribute21.6% (KL direction) and16.0% (contrast direction); the highest205 contribute63.5% and51.2%. No contexts are discarded. A few contexts can therefore materially affect a one-label estimate even when the overall reference variance is accurate.

The fourth512-document block has a contrast-direction mean about3.14 teacher-reference SEs above zero. It was not prespecified as a subgroup and must not be selected as evidence of a distinct semantic regime. Aggregate variance agreement does not explain every block fluctuation; heavy tails, multiplicity and true context effects remain possible. All four blocks and both-direction covariances are archived.

Interpretation for the user's objective hierarchy: prediction fidelity and observed-token task loss are mathematically different objectives, but detecting a reliable CE-specific correction can demand more information than detecting a KL correction. The present36-gain experiment supports that practical distinction. It does not justify optimizing noisy observed-token losses and interpreting the resulting directions as model features. Equally, it does not rule out a useful CE-oriented replacement with a proper training/validation design.

## Previous continuation: H524

## H524 — Shared and fit-dependent errors; averaging versus pooling

For every frozen H523 half-fit pair, define reconstruction errors e_common=(e_left+e_right)/2 and e_diff=(e_left−e_right)/2. Use the full-vector derivative through the residual bypass, MLP and final probability readout at each actual receiver. With Q(e)=one-half e^T F e and cross=e_common^T F e_diff, left error is Q(common)+Q(diff)+cross and right error is Q(common)+Q(diff)−cross. Their average is Q(common)+Q(diff). Pairwise local prediction KL is4Q(diff). The midpoint reconstruction has error e_common.

This is an algebraic decomposition conditional on the two fits, not a population bias/variance decomposition or identification of semantic features. The common error need not be irreducible; different data, model families or objectives may change it. We evaluate actual finite prediction KL for midpoint reconstructions on the same two reused panels, and compare with archived individual fits and H522's pooled3,072-source rank-k fit. No maps are refitted.

|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|

|PCA|144|8.03%–8.60%|8.08%–8.62%|1.0064–1.0247|0.9994–1.0053|

Ranges cover all four partitions and both panels, not confidence intervals. At rank36 only about2.2–2.6% of average local error is differential; at144 about8.0–9.0%; at576 about23.7–25.7%. Thus H523's near100% pairwise-disagreement/error ratio at576 corresponds to roughly25% removable-by-averaging error, not100%. About three quarters remains common to each pair.

Finite midpoint gains closely follow the local differential-energy prediction: their ratio is about0.999–1.013 across all tested cases. Finite symmetric pair KL is about0.986–1.002 times four local differential energy. This supports a largely local explanation for these fit-to-fit differences at the tested perturbations; it is not a global linearity claim.

Pooling data at the original rank achieves almost the midpoint's fidelity. Pooled rank36 error ranges from about0.3% lower to0.9% higher than midpoint error; at144 it is0.6–3.9% higher; at576 it is5.7–9.1% higher. The midpoint can use up to min(2k,1023) dimensions:72,288,1023 respectively. These are upper bounds, not measured numerical ranks. The pooled comparator retains36,144,576. Consequently, midpoint gains are not free compression or a matched-rank advantage, and the small difference cannot establish equivalence. Both procedures use the same total source pool through different constructions.

The findings support a shared large computation plus sample-sensitive corrections within this approximation family. They do not identify a stable semantic core or unique fundamental units. Better calibration and averaging both reduce some error, but the common remainder remains substantial and depends on the objective and rank.

Four prescribed random complementary1,536/1,536 partitions of the pooled3,072 calibration sources (seed20280106) generate eight fits per method/rank. Write-space similarity is the mean squared cosine of principal angles between orthonormal bases for each map's range. Operator difference is the Frobenius norm of A−B divided by the root mean square of the two operator Frobenius norms. The latter measures both reading and writing for oblique Fisher maps; individual eigenvector alignment is not used.

Higher-rank subspaces have higher overlap partly by dimension alone. For independent uniformly random subspaces of equal rank in1,023 dimensions the expected overlap is k/1,023; this is a geometric reference, not an assumed null distribution for the fitted maps. Symmetric prediction KL is half KL(prediction A||B) plus half KL(B||A). It measures how differently the two fits predict, whereas approximation error is their average KL from the native model. Their ratio is descriptive, not an additive error decomposition or an equivalence test.

## H508 — Individual-head reconstruction error dominates the joint gap

For each of512 natural evaluation contexts, compute the full-path probability-score tangent caused by each head's source reconstruction error. The full-path state derivative includes both direct residual and MLP contributions. Form a9×9 Gram matrix G with Gij equal to one-half the probability-weighted inner product of the two centered-logit tangents. Its diagonal is the sum of individual local errors; its off-diagonal terms capture reinforcement or cancellation. Sum every entry to obtain the local joint KL approximation.

Use the four prescribed maps: mean replacement, PCA, pooled MLP-metric, and pooled full-path-metric. All maps, contexts, and errors are frozen from H507. Compare the local sum with the previously measured finite full-path KL. This is a diagnostic on reused data, not a new causal intervention experiment or confirmation.

| Map | Local diagonal error | Net cross terms | Local joint error | Net cross fraction | Actual finite KL | Finite/local |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|mean|0.010404|0.001285|0.011689|10.99%|0.011822|1.0114|
|PCA|0.004918|0.001007|0.005925|17.00%|0.005837|0.9853|
|pooled|0.005256|0.001085|0.006341|17.11%|0.006208|0.9790|
|full_metric|0.004878|0.000972|0.005849|16.61%|0.005747|0.9825|

For full-path-metric maps, diagonal terms account for83.39% of local joint error and net cross terms16.61%. PCA and pooled MLP maps have similar net cross fractions, about17%. Thus cross-head reinforcement matters, but the larger component is individual reconstruction error. Fixing only net cross terms while leaving diagonal errors unchanged would not remove most of this measured gap. That is an arithmetic diagnostic, not an achievable intervention bound: changing a representation can change both terms.

Positive and negative cross terms coexist. For the full-path map, positive off-diagonal terms sum to0.001345 and negative terms to−0.000373, yielding net0.000972. The Gram matrices contain all pairs; no selected head pair is promoted as the complete explanation. These terms reflect overlap of output-score perturbations, not necessarily direct causal interactions between heads.

The local joint estimate closely matches finite KL: finite/local ratios range0.9790–1.0114 across the four conditions. For the compressed maps, finite KL is about1.5–2.1% below the local estimate. Strong finite nonlinear effects are therefore not needed to explain most of the aggregate joint error on this panel. Individual contexts can still differ; these are pooled comparisons, not pointwise error guarantees.

Including the direct residual path increases absolute KL substantially. Full-path PCA has KL0.005837 and50.62% normalized recovery; original Fisher0.006237 and47.24%; pooled Fisher0.006208 and47.49%. This is an important scope limit: the metric used to construct the Fisher maps differentiated the MLP route while holding the residual bypass fixed. It did not penalize errors that matter through the direct residual route. A full-path metric must differentiate both: a source-direction derivative becomes (I+J_MLP) applied to that direction before the final probability readout. The result is consistent with metric-scope mismatch, but does not by itself prove that including the bypass in fitting will fix the error. Per-head fitting and source dependence may also limit joint reconstruction.

It does not isolate finite nonlinear interaction: even a local quadratic KL has cross terms when source errors combine. Local cross-term decomposition would distinguish that explanation from stronger nonlinear effects.

## H502 — Local output sensitivity explains most of the read/write advantage

Keep the H500 donor/H499 receiver pairs and all three rank-4 source maps fixed: PCA, orthogonal projection into the Fisher write span, and the original oblique Fisher map. For each actual receiver/source pair, differentiate the MLP and final probability readout at the intact baseline. Compute one-half the probability-weighted squared centered-logit tangent for the full source and each reconstruction error. This is the leading quadratic term of KL. Divide error by effect to predict local recovery, then compare with native finite KL at prescribed intervention magnitudes 0.1, 1, and 2, both signs and all nine heads.

The residual bypass remains fixed, matching prior experiments. Derivatives include input RMS normalization, bilinear MLP, final RMS normalization, vocabulary projection, and softcap. The local prediction is sign-independent and scales quadratically with magnitude; finite behavior can depend on sign. The experiment uses local derivatives on the actual evaluation pairs as a diagnostic, not to refit any map. It is exploratory on reused data.

At magnitude 0.1, finite recovery differs from the local prediction by at most 0.35 percentage points across all heads, methods, and signs; the median difference is 0.06 points. All 18 signed head cases have the same method ordering as the local prediction. Aggregate finite KL divided by its local quadratic prediction ranges from 0.9942 to 1.0064 across effect and method-error terms. Thus the small-scale regime is consistent with the implemented local approximation.

At magnitude 1, the median recovery discrepancy is 0.57 points and the maximum is 3.90 points. At magnitude 2, these become 0.96 and 8.05 points. The largest gaps occur in heads 0 and 2. Aggregate finite/local KL ratios span 0.9465–1.0970 at unit scale and 0.9035–1.2605 at double scale. These pooled quantities do not bound every individual case.

For head 5, local recovery is 21.36% / 41.88% / 57.82% for PCA / orthogonal-write / oblique, closely matching H501's finite values of about 21–22% / 41–43% / 58%. Head 3's local values similarly predict its large two-stage improvement. The strong read/write advantage therefore does not require finite-intervention nonlinearity to explain it in these cases; it is already present in local probability sensitivity.

Finite nonlinearity still matters. At unit and double scales, method ordering changes relative to the local prediction in the positive-sign cases of heads 0, 2, and 4. These are mostly comparisons with small local ordering margins. In particular, local Fisher does not predict a universal benefit: head 0's oblique map is locally slightly worse than PCA, and head 4's local oblique recovery is also below PCA. Because these differences already exist under the evaluation-pair local metric, finite nonlinearity alone cannot explain why the training-derived maps fail to dominate there. Metric estimation from only 16 training receivers, source covariance shift, and source/receiver pairing are remaining possibilities.

This narrows the explanation: downstream probability geometry and the coordinate-reading rule explain much of the observed benefit, with finite nonlinear corrections that vary by head and scale. It does not establish that the resulting axes are unique or stable across independently estimated metrics, nor that the original network implements the approximate map as an isolated internal unit.

Audits: the float32 MLP directional derivative agrees with independent double-precision algebra to maximum relative error 7.81e-7 on the checked source direction for each head. Every unit-scale error/effect aggregate replays H500/H501 within the 1e-5 recovery tolerance. All rows are finite; the smallest saved KL is positive, about 6.48e-12. Very small individual effects can still be sensitive to floating-point error, so conclusions rely on pooled diagnostics rather than tiny per-row ratios. No documents were added; tracked total remains 19,456.

The twenty-hypothesis tournament is updated: hypothesis4 (local sensitivity explains the large gain) gains support; hypothesis5 (finite nonlinear effects) remains relevant but is not the main explanation for the strongest gains. Hypotheses14–15 (stable subspaces/operators versus unstable individual axes) now become especially relevant to claiming a canonical form.

## H501 — The retained subspace and the rule for reading its coordinates both matter

Use exactly the H500 new donor sources and H499 receiver contexts, with all fitted maps frozen. For each head, the Fisher map has a four-dimensional write subspace spanned by B C^(1/2) U. Construct an orthonormal basis Q for this same subspace and replace the oblique map by ordinary Euclidean projection Q Q^T. Compare native finite responses under PCA, this orthogonal-write control, and the original oblique Fisher map. Both signs and all nine heads are retained. This is an exploratory mechanism diagnostic on reused outcomes, not another fresh confirmation.

The control retains the Fisher-selected write subspace and removes its particular coordinate-reading rule. Orthogonal projection minimizes raw Euclidean source error within that fixed subspace. The original oblique map reads C^(-1/2) U coordinates and writes through C^(1/2) U; a source component outside the write subspace can therefore change the reconstructed coordinates. This extra freedom can preserve behavior even when it worsens raw source reconstruction.

Head 5 illustrates both contributions: PCA recovers 20.51–22.19%, ordinary projection into the Fisher-selected write subspace recovers 41.14–42.50%, and the original oblique map recovers 57.52–57.79%. Head 3 similarly progresses from 33.48–35.02%, to 50.14–53.76%, to 64.94–68.23%. These point estimates support both better subspace selection and a useful coordinate-reading rule in these heads.

The pattern is heterogeneous. In heads 1 and 2 the orthogonal-write control is roughly comparable to or slightly worse than PCA, while the oblique map is better. In heads 7 and 8 both changes help at the point-estimate level. Head 6 changes little because all maps are already highly faithful. Head 0 remains poorly captured, and head 4 shows no consistent benefit. Oblique exceeds its orthogonal-write control in 17 of 18 point comparisons; head 4 negative is the exception. No new superiority intervals were specified for this diagnostic, so these counts are descriptive, not significance claims.

Raw source reconstruction always improves or stays equal when replacing an oblique projection by the orthogonal projection onto its own write span; the numerical audit checks this. Yet behavioral recovery often falls. Consequently, a useful computational description may require a read function together with a write direction, not just an axis and its Euclidean projection coefficient. This is compatible with many equivalent coordinate systems within the retained subspace. It does not establish that these particular four axes are uniquely canonical, semantically interpretable, or fundamental to all layers.

The experiment separates selected write subspace from coordinate readout, but not every reason the readout works. Candidate explanations include local output-Fisher weighting, compensation for omitted source components, source covariance correlations, context-dependent sensitivity, and finite normalization effects. The current maps use a local metric averaged over only 16 training receivers; finite native behavior may differ from that local objective. A direct local-versus-finite diagnostic is the next informative test.

## H498 — Choosing source coordinates by their output effects

Compare the PCA source projections in H497 with a data-and-behavior-weighted map at the same ranks 4, 16, 64, and 128, separately for all nine heads. The behavior metric is the local output Fisher metric: the probability-weighted squared change in centered logits, which approximates twice the output KL for small perturbations. It includes the MLP, input and output RMS normalization, vocabulary readout, and logit softcap. The direct residual receiver is held fixed, matching the intervention definition.

Estimate this metric on 16 fixed training receivers (indices 0, 64, …, 960 from the earlier 1,024 training contexts), independently of the reused evaluation panel. In the full 128-dimensional calibration PCA coordinates, let C be calibration covariance and F the mean local Fisher matrix. Let U contain the leading eigenvectors of C^(1/2) F C^(1/2). The source reconstruction is A = C^(1/2) U U^T C^(-1/2). This rank-k map minimizes the calibration-covariance-averaged local quadratic reconstruction objective for that F. No finite evaluation loss, regularization strength, or clipping was used to select it.

This is generally an oblique projection: its read and write directions differ, and it can increase raw source norm. It has the same bottleneck rank as PCA, not the same orthogonal-projection constraint or necessarily the same parameter count. Its local optimality does not guarantee finite-KL optimality or generalization. Evaluate the same 64 donors and 512 receiving contexts, both signed unit interventions, with native downstream computation. These are exploratory reused-receiver results.

The evidence favors a distribution- and objective-dependent description with heterogeneous rank requirements, rather than a universal four-coordinate source representation. It does not yet identify fundamental semantic units or show that the remaining heads are intrinsically incompressible. ## H494 — Alignment of less stable corrections in probability space

Compare the complementary cross responses from H493's paired train-half models, retaining all four splits and both signs. Use the same512 reused H491 receivers and a common native intact baseline probability metric. For each side, the correction is its cross projection onto the complement of the principal-cosine>=.95 core. Compute three pooled alignments: (1) raw vector cosine, (2) Fisher cosine of the baseline-centered readout tangent J delta, weighted by baseline probabilities, and (3) cosine of the actual finite log-probability change log p_full−log p_core, centered and weighted by the same baseline probabilities. The third metric includes finite nonlinear changes but is not KL or a cosine of probability vectors. Also replay the actual KL(full-model||core-model) changes from H493.

Pool inner products and energies over receivers before computing cosine. These are energy-weighted alignments, not the mean per-example cosine; large events can dominate. Disagreement/mean energy is (E_left+E_right−2 inner)/[(E_left+E_right)/2]. Both sides use the same weighting distribution, so apparent alignment cannot arise merely from choosing a different metric for each side.

Across pairs/signs, raw alignment ranges 0.674–0.704, Fisher alignment 0.720–0.756, and finite log-ratio alignment 0.713–0.758. Fisher disagreement is 48.9%–56.4% of mean correction energy, but only 0.62%–1.21% of native intervention Fisher energy. These denominators answer different questions.

The corrections have meaningful common behavior and somewhat higher alignment in the probability-sensitive metric, but output sensitivity does not collapse their differences into functional identity. They are small relative to the dominant native effect while still appreciably different relative to one another. Similar total fidelity across half-data fits therefore reflects a stable dominant computation plus partly reproducible corrections; it does not establish that the entire unstable geometric tail is merely an irrelevant coordinate rotation.

This result also distinguishes three objects that should not be conflated: subspace overlap (H492), individual axis alignment after sign/permutation matching (H492), and input-dependent correction outputs under a probability metric (H494). Weak subspace/axis overlap can coexist with stronger output alignment because the dataset weights how directions are used. Conversely, raw-output overlap does not guarantee behavioral equivalence. These observations support an explicitly distribution- and metric-dependent canonical approximation, with a fidelity tolerance rather than a claim of unique universal feature axes.

## H486 — Exact rational rank1 response and necessary nonlinear terms

Use the fixed calibration top1 source direction and the same512 H484/H485 receivers, both signed donor amplitudes. This is an exploratory native-model algebra/control experiment, not fresh confirmation or a learned replacement. Direct residual path remains fixed. All recovery denominators here are native rank1 intervention effects, not the full-source effects used in H485.

For unnormalized receiver p and fixed source direction b, intervene p−a b. The bias-free bilinear write is

w(a) = (N0 + a N1 + a² N2) / (d0 + a d1 + a² d2),

where N0=D[(Lp)⊙(Rp)], N1=−D[(Lp)⊙(Rb)+(Lb)⊙(Rp)], N2=D[(Lb)⊙(Rb)], d0=mean(p²)+eps, d1=−2mean(p b), and d2=mean(b²). The Down bias cancels in the response. Use the native float32 RMS epsilon even for float64 algebra.

Writing w0=N0/d0, V1=N1−w0 d1 and V2=N2−w0 d2 gives the exact response

Δw(a) = [a V1 + a² V2] / [d0 + a d1 + a² d2].

Thus at a fixed receiver the entire response curve along this source direction lies in the span of two output vectors. Those vectors vary across receivers: this is not a global rank2 output space or a discovered pair of semantic features. It follows from the architecture, and now has numerical verification. Constructing these vectors still uses the native weights and receiver state; no computational/storage saving is established by the identity alone.

### A concrete functional-equivalence result

The learned map has the form normalized_write = centered_kernel(x) E C + intercept, with E of size768xq and C of sizeqx1152, q=64 or128. C has rank16. Factor C=U S V and combine E with U S. The resulting read matrix is768x16 and write matrix16x1152, independent of q. Kernel centering is folded into the constant intercept and an explicit row-mean correction; it is not silently discarded. Thus both training widths compile to the same final architecture and storage size, although they represent different fitted functions.

For each selected model, store shared support768x1152=884736 scalars, shared scale1, and31888 per-map scalars: read12288, write18432, intercept1152 and row-mean read correction16. A single compiled map totals916625 scalars. This is much more than '16 neurons'; the dictionary dominates cost. All six initial/selected maps were compiled and tested on128 held-out query inputs. Relative write-prediction differences are4.3e−9 to5.0e−9 in float64; rank16 truncation of the saved float32 effective matrices discards only~1.0–1.2e−8 relative matrix norm. This verifies the algebraic collapse within numerical precision. It does not verify identical downstream probabilities after arbitrary low-precision implementations, establish a runtime speedup, remove sign/degenerate-subspace ambiguity, or prove a unique global canonical form.

This directly illustrates the user's distinction: a wider training parameterization can describe the same type of final function, and unnecessary internal factorization can be removed without changing predictions. The performance experiment remains separate: same final size does not imply same function or sufficient faithfulness.

Next avoid interpreting more reused-panel tuning as confirmation. Freeze the validation-selected64/32 and128/32 maps, collect a genuinely new receiving-document panel, and evaluate intact predictions and both signed response changes with unchanged sources. Track absolute effects and error concentration as well as recovery. This separates sampling/generalization uncertainty from the narrow width/step gains before choosing another optimization branch. New source/distribution transfer is an additional question, not supplied by fresh receivers alone. Canonical-form CE comparison, source rank1/tail tests and broader-head transfer remain unresolved.

Numerical nested-feature and rank64-prefix replay audits pass. Compiled models, unfused models, complete optimization histories, per-case scores and bootstrap draws are preserved. Total12992 documents; no claim that the broad research goal is complete.

### Twenty explanations to discriminate in the canonical-form phase

These are competing or compatible hypotheses, not twenty findings. Priorities are qualitative, and selected outcomes on this reused panel are not independent confirmation.

| Explanation | Current assessment | Discriminator |
|---|---|---|
|1. State magnitude masks response differences in the loss.|Supported contributor by fixed-feature contrast fitting.|Sweep fixed normalized state/contrast weights and measure both behaviors.|
|2. Raw-write error weights the wrong output directions for probabilities.|Leading:93–94% raw versus57–62% KL recovery.|Fit finite response KL with input family held fixed.|
|3. The64 input coordinates omit important interaction directions.|Leading capacity limitation: rank64 retains training response error.|Expand input rank while fixing response objective and output budget.|
|4. Rank16 output bottleneck is the main remaining limitation.|Weakened by unrestricted rank64 witness.|Independent rank sweep and probability-weighted output selection.|
|5. Finite donor sampling inflates apparent structure.|Open; source strata are small.|Freeze maps and use new donors/receivers.|
|6. More training contexts are needed for the empirical quotient.|Open.|Independent training-size curves with fixed ranks.|
|7. Empirical kernel coordinates are less effective than native learned factors.|Open; current coordinates use a degree-two polynomial kernel.|Compare learned native multiplicative coordinates at matched budget.|
|8. State-dependent downstream sensitivity prevents one global output metric.|Plausible, supported by earlier research.|Compare global and state-conditioned response weighting.|
|9. Normalization curvature drives remaining errors.|Possible but included in exact targets.|Amplitude sweep and analytic normalization-aware contrast features.|
|10. Local derivatives are enough; finite effects create avoidable complexity.|Unresolved in this canonical family.|Train derivatives and test small/large signed amplitudes.|
|11. The useful source variable is scalar gain along a common write.|Strong source-energy evidence, behavior untested.|Rank1 source projection plus orthogonal-tail interventions.|
|12. Low-energy source directions dominate some probability effects.|Plausible.|Direct tail effects and output-sensitivity-weighted source coordinates.|
|13. Training source/context pairings limit transferable response fits.|Open.|Crossed versus paired source/context training at fixed examples.|
|14. Empirical canonical axes are unstable while their spans are stable.|Open.|Resample calibration; compare spectra, subspaces and behavior separately.|
|15. Multiple equivalent low-rank parameterizations obscure a stable function.|Algebraically compatible.|Audit functional equivalence after metric whitening and latent gauge changes.|
|16. CE needs far more independent labeled examples than distillation.|Plausible after CE validation/test mismatch.|Matched data-scaling of CE and teacher KL objectives.|
|17. Optimization failures masquerade as objective equivalence.|Supported by H467 small-step improvement.|Full-gradient finite-response loss with fixed trust steps.|
|18. An unconstrained offset separates state and contrast objectives.|Relevant limitation; contrast loss cancels constants.|Optimize/calibrate intercept separately and test state behavior.|
|19. Sparse exceptional contexts dominate pooled KL uncertainty.|Plausible given wide bands.|Report effect/error concentration, robust strata and independent replication.|
|20. Head6 compactness does not generalize to other computations.|Established scope concern.|Repeat frozen methodology on broader heads and layers.|

## H457 — Compiled finite law inside the source subspace

Reuse H454/H455128 contexts,24 sources,eight output spans and signed amplitudes. Reconstruct hhat=Hc using the frozen16 source coordinates. Let s²=mean(pre²)+epsilon, x=pre/s, d=mean((pre−alpha*hhat)²)+epsilon and M0=M_omit(x). The exact omitted response within this source subspace is ((s²−d)*M0−alpha*s*T_hhat*x+alpha²*B_omit(hhat,hhat))/d. The scalar denominator uses source-coordinate dot products and a16x16 source Gram matrix. This is an exact rational expression, not a Taylor truncation. The original source h still supplies the exact retained response; the omitted predictor uses hhat, so the combined predictor is not a single native intervention at hhat.

The baseline-normalization component (s²/d−1)*M0 remains exact outside output projection. Project the remaining linear-plus-quadratic numerator divided by d through the frozen simplified baseline output rule. Unprojected controls add both terms directly. Dense and joint256 variants differ only in the context-input linear maps. Gains versus first order combine quadratic numerator and exact normalization changes; this experiment does not separately attribute them.

### Twenty mechanistic alternatives for the amplitude effect

These alternatives can coexist. They are hypotheses, not posterior probabilities or established mechanisms. A1-A20 name this mechanistic shortlist rather than replacing the global twenty-hypothesis tournament.

|ID|Possible explanation|Experiment that would distinguish it|
|---|---|---|
|A1|Input RMS changes radial gain as edits grow.|Compare exact RMS with a frozen denominator in otherwise identical finite MLP responses.|
|A2|The source-residual angle controls the input RMS denominator.|Hold source norm fixed and vary its residual projection with paired directional controls.|
|A3|The bilinear quadratic source term changes the group relationship.|With input normalization fixed, compare full bilinear response with its first-order term.|
|A4|Final output RMS causes the distribution-dependent trend.|Linearize only final RMS while retaining logit capping and exact KL.|
|A5|The tanh logit cap changes which errors matter.|Linearize only the cap around baseline logits, retaining output RMS and exact distribution scoring.|
|A6|Softmax/KL curvature causes the trend even for linear MLP responses.|Compare exact KL and baseline Fisher scoring of the same linear response; then isolate normalization and cap.|
|A7|A few baseline logit margins determine sensitivity to nonlinear scoring.|Stratify by frozen margin bins and validate on a separate recipient panel.|
|A8|Natural and Gaussian source norm tails differ.|Use controls with matched radial distributions and separately audited directional moments.|
|A9|Directional fourth moments matter even at matched norms.|Compare covariance-matched spherical-direction controls with natural directions within narrow norm bins.|
|A10|Source coefficient skewness creates asymmetric finite responses.|Pair positive and negative source edits; odd-order effects should reverse differently from even-order effects.|
|A11|Finite sampled Gaussian covariance mismatch is sufficient.|Use exactly whitened/recolored Gaussian-derived batches and paired assignment controls.|
|A12|Finite sampled Gaussian mean mismatch is sufficient.|Center each sampled batch to the donor mean while retaining its original covariance, then compare to uncentered draws.|
|A13|Token-position mixtures conceal opposing mechanisms.|Estimate the predeclared contrast separately by position with simultaneous uncertainty and independent replication.|
|A14|The fixed donor calibration pool is atypical.|Repeat calibration using a new disjoint donor pool without changing selected groups or contrast.|
|A15|A small set of recipient documents dominates the effect.|Measure influence and report robust or trimmed sensitivity separately without replacing the original statistic.|
|A16|Recipient-conditioned response operators interact with donor assignment.|Average controlled source ensembles within fixed recipients; compare with pooled assignment estimates.|
|A17|The added factors compensate for core errors only along some directions.|Hold the core fixed and evaluate signed cross-response structure across independently selected directional strata.|
|A18|The effect is specific to the selected core/add partition.|Repeat the frozen contrast for independently chosen matched-size partitions; distinguish selection effects from universal grouping.|
|A19|The effect is specific to head6 or layer17.|Use a new selection panel for another source/layer, followed by separate confirmation.|
|A20|Higher-order semantic organization contributes beyond these geometric mechanisms.|After moment and nonlinear-scoring controls, use controlled linguistic edits with predicted, held-out behavior; current Gaussian comparisons alone cannot establish this.|

Floating-point artifacts remain an implementation alternative rather than a proposed model mechanism; exact scaling, row replay, native-epsilon derivatives and partition audits constrain that possibility but do not substitute for scientific controls.

Its advantage over Fisher128 is0.110332,[0.088181,0.132483], and over mean core+random64 is0.151797,[0.129646,0.173948]; both frozen5-point superiority gates pass. The90% recovery gate fails. Advantage over individual-energy128 is0.029631,[0.007480,0.051782]: this interval is positive, but its lower bound does not clear the predeclared2-point threshold, so that gate still fails. Report the positive comparison without silently relaxing the gate.

Head6 native unit effect KL is0.00195622. At4× amplitude, residual128 recovery is0.789565 versus Fisher1280.685149 and energy1280.764176; these stress comparisons are descriptive. Unit clamp remaining fraction is0.188264, with no new clamp-threshold confirmation claimed. Exact groups, primary thresholds, and native vectors remained frozen from H410.

Transfer is heterogeneous. Residual128 recovery for the eight other heads ranges0.406987–0.842506. Head8 has the highest point recovery,0.842506,[0.757006,0.928006] in the joint16 band. Head5 has0.406987,[0.321487,0.492488]. Thus the group is not uniquely head6-specific, but it does not transfer at uniformly high fidelity. Both all-eight transfer gates fail. Six other heads (0,1,2,3,4,7) have simultaneous recovery upper bounds below.8, and head5 is below.5; head8's interval crosses.8.

Residual additions improve over Fisher128 at every other head in the point estimates, but simultaneous intervals clear the predeclared5-point advantage only for head3 (gain0.185560,[0.100060,0.271061]) and head4 (gain0.446315,[0.360815,0.531816]). The other six intervals include zero. This is a family-controlled transfer pattern, not evidence of a uniform improvement. For head4, individual-energy128 has descriptively higher recovery0.576365 than residual1280.508205; the raw-energy comparator remains important.

Absolute effects differ substantially: head5 unit KL is0.00002713, head7 0.00005984, head6 0.00195622, and head8 0.00033332. Recovery fractions should not be read as shares of total model computation. These are MLP-path source interventions in one layer/model and one text distribution, not complete head ablations, semantic labels or a globally compressed model.

Interpretation: a fixed native group can transfer across documents and partly across sources, but its usefulness has a structured source dependence. Compensation-aware selection corrects a particular attribution failure without establishing an elementary semantic unit. The striking head3/head4 rescue suggests the added64 factors may supply different roles for different sources: compensating the core for head6, while carrying a larger direct share elsewhere. That last explanation is a hypothesis, not established by the current KL tables.

Next highest-information diagnostic: separate the fixed Fisher64 core and the fixed64 residual-selected additions across all nine sources, without selecting any new factors. Measure each component's native Fisher energy, its mutual cross term, and the omitted remainder; pair this with finite retained prediction/clamping for core-only, additions-only and their union. This can distinguish a source-dependent compensator from a generally useful standalone component and directly test the head3/head4 interpretation. Predeclare simultaneous bands across all nine sources. Then, if these group roles prove structured, construct the broader source-by-independently-selected-group transfer matrix; do not jump from pooled fidelity to semantic names.

### Updated hypothesis tournament: twenty explanations and discriminating tests

Priorities are qualitative, not numerical posterior probabilities. Several explanations can coexist.

|#|Explanation|Current evidence|Discriminating test|
|---|---|---|---|
|1|Learned source orientations align with high-sensitivity directions of the local MLP.|Leading; broad discovery and fresh selected-pair confirmation.|Predict advantage from Jacobian geometry on unseen contexts.|
|2|The low coupling ratio is only head6 dominating a sum.|Weakened by fresh separate-source normalization.|Retain per-source normalization across more pairs.|
|3|A few native bilinear factors carry the sensitivity advantage.|Unresolved, mechanistically actionable.|Freeze factor ranking on old documents and test retained/removed sets on held-out documents.|
|4|The advantage is distributed across many factors.|Strong alternative to3.|Measure held-out reconstruction and ablation curves against matched random sets.|

Thus the selected low K/J ratios are driven chiefly by much larger first-order sensitivity, not demonstrated suppression of absolute curvature.

A supplementary algebraic diagnostic reconstructs each head's first-order energy from the complete pair-sum system. All reconstructed energies are positive; pair-sum replay differs by at most2.98e-8 in absolute squared-energy units. In actual heads0/6, head6 contributes98.793% of the pair's common-scaled first-order energy; for heads5/6,99.717%. Corresponding rotated fractions are91.101% and97.859%. This exposes a serious interpretation limit: a low ratio to summed first-order energy can be dominated by one source. It does not establish balanced independence between two equally responsive sources. The diagnostic does not change the preregistered metric or candidate selection.

Normalization cancellation also differs across pairs. For heads0/6, full mixed energy divided by the sum of fixed-scale and correction energies is0.555 actual versus0.536 rotated; for heads5/6,0.742 versus0.635. Those pairs remain included; no exclusions or narrowed post-hoc band are used. This limits universal conclusions, while the predeclared selected-pair results survive the full band.

Hypothesis update: enhanced first-order sensitivity along natural source orientations is a broad within-model pattern; relative mixed-curvature suppression is supported for a subset, not universally. Selected low ratios may reflect unequal source sensitivity rather than pair-specific decoupling. Head-associated local operators remain useful quantitative descriptions, but the current evidence is insufficient to call the head pair an independent or semantic computational unit.

This supports a local explanation for the selected source pairs: learned orientations can have large first-order response energy while mixed curvature is comparatively modest relative to that sensitivity. The mixed Taylor operator predicts the ordinary-amplitude interaction well for actual and rotated directions alike. At larger amplitudes, nonlinear evolution of both individual-response energy and mixed interaction matters. The result does not show that the mixed vector is sparse in native factors, shared across contexts, semantically interpretable or a fundamental computational unit. These are two selected pairs on a reused panel, so the orientation-specific conclusion requires broader coverage.

Hypothesis update: a local derivative-plus-mixed-curvature description is predictively useful for these joint interventions at ordinary scale. A scalar response-gain explanation is incomplete, while the first-order-normalized curvature contrast gives a concrete, testable refinement. Exact-denominator-only resummation is insufficient at large amplitude. Generic Taylor behavior explains the small-amplitude success but does not by itself explain the actual-versus-rotation curvature-to-sensitivity ratios.

Next high-information experiment: map the local mixed-curvature energy relative to first-order source energy across all36 head pairs, using full-Gram-preserving rotations and a fixed simultaneous comparison. At infinitesimal equal amplitudes, the shared amplitude factor cancels from the actual/control ratio, allowing a cheap derivative-only screen. Keep both absolute mixed-curvature energy and first-order energy alongside their ratio. This tests whether the two selected pairs reflect a broad learned orientation pattern or a restricted exception. Any selected pattern should then be confirmed on fresh documents and examined for native-factor support and cross-context transfer, rather than naming a local Taylor coefficient a semantic unit.

## H401 — Can local derivatives predict orientation-dependent response gain?

Reuse H400’s512-document panel and six geometry-preserving rotation draws, extending each selected pair(1,8),(6,8) to all four amplitude combinations(1,1),(1,−1),(4,4),(4,−4). The panel is no longer fresh for this analysis. Compare three analytic energy predictors without finite-target fits: first-order a*m1; first-order divided by exact input RMS denominator q(a); second-order a*m1+a²*m2. Here m1=N1 and m2=N2−2alpha*N1 are local input-normalized MLP Taylor coefficients. Predicted energy sums the squared norms of the two predicted individual responses.

Finite individual-response energy I and native joint composition error E are evaluation quantities. All site energies use the same intact-state squared norm for scaling. Outcome: cached native-KL audit and raw unit99 gates pass. Both universal stage-suppression gates fail. The cache audit agrees to6.94e-17 and regenerated single-source geometry agrees exactly. All raw/unit pooled squared-error ratios lie between0.00006604 and0.00147285 (0.006604–0.147285%); the largest simultaneous upper bound is0.00168628 (0.168628%). Thus approximate additivity is already present before final RMS and readout for ordinary signed removals, including matched control sources. These are squared-error fractions: their square roots range approximately0.81–3.84%, so they must not be described as sub0.15% vector-norm error.

Final normalization changes relative error by factors0.585–2.029. Under the joint72 band, five of36 normalization contrasts significantly amplify relative error, three suppress it, and28 remain unresolved. The native readout changes relative error by factors0.516–6.689:25 significantly amplify, four suppress, and seven remain unresolved. These are dimensionless changes between differently defined metrics, not an additive causal decomposition. Neither stage is a universal error suppressor. In particular, for actual heads0/6, the native readout amplifies relative error by roughly6.3–6.7× across the four amplitude conditions.

Heads1/6 illustrate why source and sign matter. At(4,4), actual raw squared-error fraction is1.439%, after RMS2.062%, and native KL3.632%. Moment controls progress2.248%→4.312%→2.426%; donor controls2.317%→4.702%→2.467%. Controls therefore have larger raw and normalized relative errors, yet smaller native relative errors. A ranking based only on native recovery would reverse the raw-space ranking. This is a readout-dependent comparison, not evidence that control source computations are inherently more independent.

The common-scale raw-error diagnostic removes the intervention-effect denominator. For heads1/6 at(4,4), moment/actual error ratio is2.261, joint interval[1.887,2.710]; donor/actual2.682,[2.238,3.215]. At(4,−4), the ordering reverses: moment/actual0.721,[0.602,0.864], donor/actual0.811,[0.676,0.972]. Across all24 common-scale comparisons, eight significantly favor actual sources (controls have more error), five favor controls, and eleven are unresolved. No universal actual-source independence is supported. The sign reversal persists without dividing by each intervention's own effect size.

Hypothesis update: generic weak cross-source interaction at ordinary amplitudes is supported in raw space, not just in the output metric. Universal normalization/readout suppression is contradicted on this panel. Sign-dependent coupling and metric-dependent ordering remain important. The architecture's exact single-direction rational law is useful, but neither its algebraic compactness nor high native recovery identifies semantic units. These outcomes remain local to L17, three selected head pairs, reused documents and the stated control construction.

Next discriminating experiment: test the leading generic explanation against source organization by expanding to all36 head pairs with a cheap raw-space interaction screen, retaining actual and matched moment controls, both signs and ordinary/larger amplitudes. Freeze a criterion for unusually weak or strong coupling relative to controls, account for multiple comparisons and source effect balance, and confirm selected pairs on fresh documents before detailed output scoring. This broadens source coverage instead of extrapolating the three selected pairs. A separate full-geometry matched control would be needed to isolate mutual-angle effects; current controls do not provide that isolation. Subsequent native-factor sparsity or cross-context transfer tests should target reproducible exceptional pairs, if any, rather than calling every locally accurate response law a discovered computational feature.

Hypothesis update: the generic-small-intervention explanation remains strong; special actual-source additivity is weakened; behavior-metric/effect-size explanations gain priority. Evidence for mixed directions outside the single-source span remains intact from H395, but the importance of those directions depends on the readout and normalization. Raw-response balance can change comparative conclusions, so universal claims of learned source independence are unwarranted.

Next high-information experiment: separate interaction size at three stages—raw MLP output, final-normalized residual, and native output distribution—using explicit common scales as well as intervention-relative recovery. Compare actual and matched controls with source-balance and mutual-angle summaries. This can distinguish intrinsically weak bilinear interactions from normalization/readout suppression and denominator-driven recovery changes. Use the same fixed head pairs initially for diagnosis, then fresh documents and broader pairs for any selected claim. A recipient-metric fit of the mixed response in the single-source span remains a separate test of whether novel Euclidean directions are behaviorally necessary; it must be labeled an oracle, not feature prediction.

## Previous continuation: H395


## H395 — Do single-source response laws compose?

H394 established a rational identity along one intervention direction. H395 tests simultaneous interventions on actual head pairs (0,1), (0,6), (1,6), at eight frozen signed amplitude combinations on the reused 512-document/2,048-site H390 panel. Only the MLP response changes; the direct residual remains intact. This tests composition within this layer/model and does not establish semantic feature identities.

For directions h and k, let alpha_h=mean(p h)/s0², beta_h=mean(h²)/s0², gamma=mean(h k)/s0², s0²=mean(p²)+epsilon. Define N_h(a)=a*m1_h+a²*(m2_h+2*alpha_h*m1_h), and similarly N_k(b). The joint denominator is q=1+2a*alpha_h+2b*alpha_k+a²*beta_h+b²*beta_k+2ab*gamma. With M0 the intact bias-free bilinear MLP output, C=2B(h,k)/s0²−2gamma*M0, the exact joint change is [N_h(a)+N_k(b)+ab*C]/q. The constant output bias cancels in this response. Apply exact final RMS and native unembedding/cap/softmax for every method.

Five frozen methods: sum_single sums the two separate finite responses; shared_denominator uses (N_h+N_k)/q; norm_cross_only adds only −2ab*gamma*M0 to that numerator; projected_cross adds ab times the Euclidean projection of C onto the four local single-direction vectors; full_joint adds the complete ab*C. The projection is an analytic mixed-vector oracle, not an independently learned coefficient predictor. It tests whether additional output directions matter and does not identify the best subspace under native KL. The omission methods are operational counterfactuals; their differences are not an additive causal decomposition.

Frozen gates: {'exact_kl': True, 'double_identity': True, 'sum_single_99': False, 'shared_denominator_99': False, 'projected_cross_99': False}. Each method has its own joint24 band; no familywise claim across all five methods is made. All gates and amplitude pairs were saved before outcomes.

Outcome: the exact joint identity passes both arithmetic gates (maximum native KL 1.30591e-11; double-precision relative response error 1.11468e-13). All three frozen approximate-method 99% gates fail across the full amplitude grid. These failures are retained rather than replacing the threshold with one suggested by the results.

At the ordinary signed unit combinations (1,1) and (1,−1), summing the separate laws recovers 99.722–99.964% of the native KL effect. Its minimum simultaneous lower bound at those combinations is 99.133%, using the already-defined band over all24 cases. Thus substantial within-source nonlinearity can coexist with weak cross-source interaction at ordinary removal amplitudes. This is a secondary reading of the frozen grid, not a new gate or independent confirmation.

The difficult pair is heads1/6 at (4,4): recovery is 96.368% for separate laws, 94.983% for the shared denominator, 93.356% for normalization-cross-only, and 97.503% for the projected mixed term. Exact mixed response restores numerical agreement. Correcting only one coupling can therefore worsen the approximation; normalization and bilinear contributions can compensate. Adding the complete mixed response matters here, but the deficit is much smaller than the previously observed failure of first-order prediction along one source at large amplitude.

The mixed vector's Euclidean relative residual after projection onto the four single-direction vectors has median0.59237, 95th percentile0.88594 and maximum0.99450. These are norm fractions, not squared energy fractions. Mixed responses often introduce substantial new directions, while their effect on native output distributions can remain small. Projected-cross recovery spans97.503–99.995%; its universal99% gate fails. This does not prove the four-vector span cannot achieve99% under a native-KL-optimized fit: the implemented projection minimizes Euclidean mixed-vector error. Nor does it prove any new direction is a semantic feature. Local independence, output-metric redundancy and limited intervention magnitude remain competing explanations.

The maximum single-document share of baseline KL over the24 cases is4.704%. This supplementary diagnostic does not exclude heavy error concentration or masking within documents. Pair controls, broader head coverage, fresh documents and earlier layers remain needed for broader claims.

### Twenty hypotheses after the composition test

These are competing, sometimes compatible explanations; priorities are qualitative, not posterior probabilities. The present experiment is restricted to three actual L17 head pairs. Proposed follow-ups below are not preregistered results.

|#|Hypothesis and reason|Discriminating experiment|Priority/evidence|
|---|---|---|---|
|1|Single-source rational laws are useful local computational units because cross-source interaction is weak.|Confirm sum-of-laws prediction on fresh documents and more head pairs.|Leading operational hypothesis; not semantic identity.|
|2|Weak interaction is generic at these perturbation norms, rather than learned source separation.|Joint moment/donor controls matched to actual norms and angles.|Leading alternative; current actual-only experiment cannot distinguish.|
|3|Different head output subspaces have unusually weak bilinear coupling.|Compare cross-tensor energy between source subspaces against matched random subspaces.|Plausible; contextual results alone are insufficient.|
|4|Normalization coupling explains most composition error.|Compare shared-denominator and separate-denominator models over larger panels and amplitude scales.|Directly probed, but improvements need not be universal.|
|5|The mixed numerator adds directions absent from the single laws.|Measure mixed-vector projection residual and behavioral error after projection.|Directly probed; vector residual and KL importance must be distinguished.|
|6|Novel mixed directions are mostly invisible to the current output distribution.|Compare Euclidean residual energy with probability-weighted output energy.|High-information next diagnostic.|
|7|Mixed response is redundant specifically under the native output metric.|Fit mixed vector in the four-vector span using recipient probability geometry, then score finite outputs.|Plausible; Euclidean projection does not settle this.|
|8|Apparent additivity comes from domination by one source's effect.|Stratify by single-source effect balance and inspect symmetric pairs.|Important alternative.|
|9|Cancellation makes opposite-sign combinations unusually fragile.|Compare matched effect sizes and denominator behavior across signs.|Signed grid probes this; rare cancellation remains possible.|
|10|Aggregate recovery hides a small set of strongly interacting documents.|Inspect per-document excess error and effect-weighted tails; confirm selected patterns on fresh data.|Important robustness check.|
|11|Coupling emerges only when many sources change together.|Extend exact quadratic numerator to 3–9 heads and compare pairwise versus independent approximations.|Plausible; pairwise success is not many-source success.|
|12|Three selected heads are atypical.|Test all36 head pairs with frozen metrics and joint uncertainty.|Strong scope limitation.|
|13|L17 is more separable than earlier layers.|Repeat matched actual/control pair tests at earlier depths.|High priority for model-wide claims.|
|14|Exact final RMS hides substantial interaction in raw MLP space.|Compare raw response norms, final normalized response and native KL.|Plausible metric dependence.|

## Previous continuation: H394


## H394 — Exact rational response law along a fixed source direction

For intact pre-MLP residual p and direction h=−payload, define s0²=mean(p²)+epsilon, alpha=mean(p h)/s0², beta=mean(h²)/s0², and q(a)=1+2 alpha a+beta a². Let m1,m2 be the first two local Taylor coefficients of the input-normalized bilinear MLP response, excluding the fixed output bias. The derived predictor is

Delta_MLP(a) = [a m1 + a²(m2+2 alpha m1)] / q(a).

Add this predicted MLP-only change to the intact final raw state, then apply final RMS, unembedding, logit cap and softmax exactly. The direct residual p stays fixed. Prediction uses intact context, payload and native weights to calculate local coefficients; no finite target response or amplitude-specific fit enters prediction.

Derivation: the input-normalized homogeneous bilinear map is (M0+a N1+a²N2)/q(a). Its Taylor coefficients imply N1=m1+2 alpha M0 and N2=m2+2 alpha m1+beta M0. Subtracting M0 cancels the baseline numerator and yields the formula above. The input RMS epsilon is included in s0²; the constant MLP output bias cancels in the response and remains in the final state. Thus this is an architecture-dependent real-arithmetic identity, not an empirical low-rank discovery.

Validate on the reused H390512-document panel:39 head/response conditions,2,048 sites, signed amplitudes−4,−1,0.5,1,2,4,8. Negative amplitudes increase the source contribution; large positive amplitudes overshoot removal. Full-panel float32 coefficients and native MLP responses are scored through double-precision unembedding/KL. A separate float64 identity check uses four fixed sites per condition at every amplitude, with the native float32 RMS epsilon explicitly retained.

This resolves why second-order Taylor truncation broke down at large amplitudes: the input-normalization denominator generates higher orders that can be summed exactly. Two local response vectors plus two scalar geometry coefficients encode this one context-specific, direction-specific trajectory. The baseline, native weights and output transformation remain necessary. This is neither global rank-two compression nor evidence of two semantic features. The architecture implies the identity; the experiment verifies the implementation and its native-precision consequences.

The next discriminating experiment is simultaneous intervention on two source heads. Compare the sum of separate finite responses, a shared-denominator predictor built from the two single-source laws, and the exact joint law including the mixed bilinear numerator. This separates errors from normalization coupling and cross-source bilinear interaction. Use fixed head pairs and signed amplitude combinations, audit the full joint identity, and measure the behavioral cost of omitting each coupling. A mixed term's formal existence alone does not establish its behavioral importance or irreducibility. Subsequent projection tests can ask whether that mixed response lies in the span of the four single-direction vectors. These hypotheses and experiment choices precede viewing any joint-intervention outcomes.

The input-normalized bilinear MLP has a quadratic numerator divided by q(a)=1+2 alpha a+beta a². If m1,m2 are its first two local Taylor response coefficients, algebra gives the exact real-arithmetic MLP response along that path:

Delta_MLP(a) = [a m1 + a²(m2+2 alpha m1)] / [1+2 alpha a+beta a²].

Apply final RMS exactly after adding this response to the intact state. This expression predicts all finite amplitudes using two context/payload-specific vectors and two input-geometry scalars; it does not require evaluating the finite input-normalized MLP at prediction time. It follows from the homogeneous bilinear architecture, not from newly learned semantic features, and does not compress the global weight tensor. In particular, source angle/norm-matched controls share these input-geometry scalars at a site while their response vectors differ.

Results and interpretation: all three frozen gates FAIL. Tail shuffling has positive point loss in all 36 settings (4.60–18.44 percentage points), but only 30/36 simultaneous lower bounds exceed zero and 11/36 exceed five points. Therefore neither a universal positive loss nor the stronger universal five-point loss is established at the declared multiplicity. This failure is retained. The protected top32 tokens carry 81.47% of recipient probability mass on average.

The clearest signal is interaction, one of the five prespecified contrasts included in the joint band. Interaction is positive in all 36 simultaneous intervals: points 8.57–89.86 percentage points, smallest lower bound 2.88 points. At rank64 the interaction spans 37.89–89.86 points. Original G/b recovers 72.72–85.99%, fully tail-shuffled G/b recovers 59.76–76.10%, original G with shuffled b recovers 33.02–39.57%, and shuffled G with original b recovers 29.66–59.52%. Geometry-minus-RHS contributions vary by basis: −2.61 to +7.98 points for probability axes, versus −21.43 to −8.55 points for the random basis. Thus no universal dominance holds across bases. A factorial average can hide large changes of sign depending on which other component is used. These are properties of the diagnostic fitting procedure, not a causal allocation of model computation between geometry and a signal generator.

Mixed-system coefficient norms reveal severe extrapolation despite accurate linear solves. Maximum squared coefficient/target-displacement norm ratio is 41,111 in the probability basis and 69,881 in the random basis, both in original-G/shuffled-b rank64 fits. The corresponding coherent original/fully-shuffled rank64 maxima are only 13.04/20.72 and 17.87/18.34. Original-G/shuffled-b rank64 selects the zero step on 5.09%/3.42% of sites (probability/random). These are retained failures, not exclusions. Very large norms and the finite safeguard mediate some of the mismatch penalty; they do not prove semantic content in individual tail directions.

Hypothesis update: (1) keeping only top32 identities while randomizing the rest is not point-equivalent to the native fit, though the universal five-point criterion fails; (2) covariance and target cross-moment consistency is strongly supported as important for oracle recovery; (3) a unique dominant factor is not supported across both bases; (4) generic tail stabilization remains plausible because this experiment changed both statistical structure and consistency in its mixed arms; (5) semantic tail features remain unproven. H384's twenty-hypothesis table remains current with these refinements.

## H342 — Context interaction versus edit curvature

Reused H339 head6 recipients and six realizations each of moment and donor controls; reused the H341 intact-state output metric. The four output modes [0, 2, 5, 1] were selected on this same panel in H341. This is exploratory decomposition, not independent confirmation.

For the quadratic compiler f, normalized intact input x, normalized edited input x+d, and frozen discovery mean μ, decompose the exact response as Df(μ)d + 2B(x−μ,d) + B(d,d). These are mean-linear, context-linear, and edit-quadratic terms. Their sum replays the compiler coefficient difference. The mean/context split depends on μ; edit-quadratic describes curvature in normalized input coordinates, not curvature along the raw residual intervention.

|Modes|Control|Mean-linear excess allocation|Context-linear excess allocation|Edit-quadratic excess allocation|Fidelity without edit-quadratic|
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|all|moment|9.27%|88.57%|2.16%|99.56%|

|top4|moment|1.53%|95.01%|3.47%|99.41%|
|top4|donor|-1.34%|97.11%|4.22%|99.35%|

Signed allocations split interactions equally and divide by control-minus-actual total energy. They are not causal percentages. Fidelity is 1−energy(omitted quadratic term)/energy(full response), using the local intact-state Fisher metric.

## H314 — Explicit cross-input kernel versus additive input predictor

For each18 head/payload group fit kernel ridge on3072 reference sites from first768 discovery documents, predicting cached missing cross responses after H300 refined64. Same targets and reference count for both representations, but different feature dimensions/inductive biases; not equal parameter capacity.

Let u be projection of centered state onto frozen core96 and v its component orthogonal to core96 and partner64. Interaction feature is phi(x,z)=u_z⊗v_z−u_x⊗v_x. Its kernel is evaluated by four products of inner products, without materializing the full tensor. Additive features concatenate midpoint and difference of u and v, each block normalized by reference mean squared norm. Each complete kernel is normalized to reference mean diagonal1. The interaction kernel is a linear model in the exact bilinear cross-product representation, so its advantage would support the relevant inductive bias, not discovery that this known bilinear model has interactions. Native output coefficients are not used in the fitted readout; targets remain native-supervised.

Missing state-dependent interactions, downstream metric mismatch and optimization/model-class limitations remain open. No semantic unit, unique ontology or intrinsic dimension has been identified.

**Interpretation.** Useful natural-state predictions do not imply faithful source-

native/compiled error and vocabulary logit fixed; change only softmax temperature
for chart construction and evaluation, with matched and crossed temperatures.
If apparent compactness changes at the same internal computation, it is partly a
property of the behavioral metric. Report exact KL, candidate probability mass,
finite versus small-scale effects; this is a diagnostic altered readout, not an
improved native model. After establishing that boundary, return to forward-
computable coefficient prediction or causal source mediation, rather than declaring
readout directions to be MLP features. Broad research goal remains active.

## Previous continuation: H255


## H255 — Local behavioral compactness depends on entropy, not strongly on candidate truncation

H254 was concrete progress: equal-norm random/shuffled controls separated generic
readout sensitivity from additional native-error alignment. H255 tests whether
H253's compact oracle corrections mainly benefit concentrated predictions or are
an artifact of keeping only256 candidate tokens.

Before outcomes, fix supports64/256/1024 and ranks16/64. Each chart is selected
from the compiled state's predicted distribution and exact score gradients; all
charts are constructed before native residual computation. Corrections still use
oracle native error coefficients. Exact full-vocabulary KL evaluates every result.
Entropy bins are fixed in nats: low<2, medium[2,4), high>=4. Reuse128 H252 documents,
512 sites; bootstrap2000 whole documents retaining all sites, including masks.
No winning support or rank is selected. A prior reporting typo about left singular
vectors does not apply: code uses right singular vectors in residual coordinates.

| Compiled entropy | Sites | Local16: support64 | support256 | support1024 | Local64: support1024 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
|All|512|77.63%|78.83%|79.28%|89.16%|
|Low (<2 nats)|172|92.09%|92.86%|93.09%|96.77%|
|Medium (2–4)|177|82.70%|83.77%|84.06%|92.47%|
|High (>=4)|163|57.78%|59.55%|60.41%|77.96%|

Values are ratio-of-sums KL error recovery relative to the compiled baseline
WITHIN each stratum, not uniform averages of per-site recovery ratios. All-support
rank16 range1.65 points; high-entropy range2.63 points. The locked <=5-point
support-stability gate passes overall and in all eligible bins. At support1024,
low-minus-high rank16 recovery is32.68 points, document-bootstrap95%[27.78,37.85],
passing the locked >=15-point entropy-dependence gate. This is an observational
stratum contrast, not a causal effect of entropy alone.

Top64/256/1024 retain mean86.50/92.90/96.95% probability mass overall. High-entropy
mass rises67.65→82.34→92.31%; low-entropy mass98.69→99.39→99.75%. Increasing support
therefore materially expands high-entropy coverage but barely closes its rank16
recovery gap. Exact full Fisher remains untested: even1024 candidates omit mass.
Wrong-context16 recovery at support1024 is9.05% low,12.85% medium,−2.61% high;
matched context still matters within each stratum. Negative recovery means the
correction increases KL. Prior H253 support256 numerical results reproduce.

Observed rank32 gap26.87pp is reproduced by whole-document shuffle gaps26.76–26.82pp; rank128 observed44.68pp is reproduced by44.64–44.69pp. Thus the original block boundaries are unnecessary for the large transfer gap in these three controls. This weakens a block-specific population-shift explanation while retaining document dependence and empirical high-dimensional variation.

**Interpretation.** Generic readout geometry plus concentrated predictions explains
a large part of apparent local compactness. Broader candidate support does not
remove the entropy dependence. This strengthens T13 objective-dependent relevance
and qualifies T09 conditional charts: strong pooled behavior does not imply equally
compact interfaces at uncertain sites. It does not show that internal MLP features
are merely tokens, nor that entropy causes the difference; error direction, size,
context and probability tails covary. Random-error controls from H254 provide
complementary evidence, not an additive explanation of these percentages.

**Next locked comparison to replicate.** Use a fresh128-document panel disjoint by
complete-document token hash from1024 discovery, original64 test and current128
test. Freeze support256 and ranks16/64 as the original H253 protocol, not the best
H255 variant. Repeat native, three isotropic and three shuffled equal-norm controls
at scales.1/1, matched/wrong charts, and fixed entropy bins. Test generic sufficiency,
additional native alignment and entropy dependence jointly. Document-level
bootstrap; same-corpus freshness only. A new population could weaken any current
account. Coefficient prediction and cost-efficient routing remain open.

Four directly relevant tests pass (stratified bootstrap arithmetic, projection,
score-gradient and reconstruction); full suite not rerun. Figure generated and
visually inspected. All H255 runs complete; broad research goal remains active.

## Previous continuation: H254


## H254 — Generic readout geometry explains much, with extra native-error alignment

Previous turn H253 made progress: new oracle correction evidence and updated
records. H254 tests whether those local charts identify MLP-specific computational
organization or mostly reflect generic downstream sensitivity.

Freeze H253 compiled states and top256-probability rank16/64 local charts. Compare
actual native-minus-compiled residual, three independent isotropic Gaussian draws,
and three document-shifted residual controls. Each control is rescaled to the
native residual norm at EACH site. Shuffling preserves token position and uses a
fixed random nonzero cyclic document offset, not a uniform arbitrary permutation.
Compare scales .1 and1. Synthetic target distributions are head(state+scaled control
error), not native predictions. Measure exact KL(target || corrected distribution),
normalized by each family's own uncorrected KL. Corrections are oracle projections;
charts precede native-error computation. Wrong-context charts shift one document.
No true next-token labels enter this experiment. Same128 documents/512 sites reused.

| Scale | Error family | Local16 KL recovered | Wrong16 KL recovered | Local64 KL recovered |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
|.1|Native|81.4%|7.3%|90.2%|
|.1|Isotropic|66.9%|9.5%|81.7%|
|.1|Shuffled residual|73.1%|15.0%|85.3%|
|1|Native|78.8%|7.1%|88.7%|
|1|Isotropic|61.7%|9.2%|77.9%|
|1|Shuffled residual|67.4%|14.0%|81.3%|

Control summaries pool KL numerator/denominator across the three seeds before
forming recovery (ratio of sums), not arithmetic averages of seed recovery ratios.
The config's shorthand 'seed-averaged recovery' means this pooling; implementation
and reported values retain that explicit distinction. Bootstrap2000 resamples
whole documents jointly across families/seeds, conditional on these three draws.

At full scale native-minus-isotropic recovery is17.12 percentage points, paired
95% interval[14.14,19.86]; native-minus-shuffled11.45[8.19,14.45]. At .1 scale the
gaps are14.47[11.92,16.97] and8.32[5.86,10.51]. Native alignment advantage is
nonzero on this panel. The locked native-specialness gate nevertheless FAILS:
required >=10 points against both controls at BOTH scales; the small-scale
shuffled gap is8.32 points. Generic-sufficiency gate PASSES: isotropic local16
recovery >=60% and matched-minus-wrong >=40 points at both scales. The full-scale
isotropic recovery interval[58.40,64.92]% straddles60%; the gate was a point-estimate
criterion, not a confidence-bound criterion. Neither gate is an ontological proof.

**Scientific update.** Much of H253's local-chart advantage occurs even for isotropic
errors, supporting generic probability-weighted readout geometry. Native residuals
also align more strongly with these directions than equal-norm shuffled residuals,
supporting an additional context/error relationship. These contributions coexist;
the percentages are not an additive causal decomposition. Random/shuffled errors
may be off the natural manifold; the .1-scale result limits, but does not eliminate,
that concern. Local sufficiency does not identify MLP semantic features or predict
missing coefficients. Prior32 tests plus H253/H254 gives34-test inventory; four
directly relevant tests passed in this run, not the entire suite.

**Next information-gain experiment.** Freeze top64/256/1024 probability-support
variants at ranks16/64 and evaluate recovery by fixed compiled-entropy strata.
If gains collapse at high entropy or vary strongly with support, a sparse likely-
token readout account strengthens. Stable gains would support broader conditional
sensitivity structure. Then replicate the frozen comparison on distinct documents
before investing in coefficient prediction. Do not tune a winning rank/support on
this reused evaluation panel. No model weights or compiled program changed.
All H254 runs complete; research goal remains active.
